#9798. 7 Ways to Build Stronger Relationships at Work

Author Upgrade Your Mindset, Rethink Imposter Syndrome. Scaling products ￫ Scaling thinking. Former AVP Engg @Swiggy

Author Upgrade Your Mindset, Rethink Imposter Syndrome. Scaling products ￫ Scaling thinking. Former AVP Engg @Swiggy

Author Upgrade Your Mindset, Rethink Imposter Syndrome. Scaling products ￫ Scaling thinking. Former AVP Engg @Swiggy

When you work with someone who doesn’t get you, there’s friction, misunderstanding, confusion and a feeling of lack of support. Conversations go around in circles, unnecessary disagreements pop up and the lack of camaraderie makes work feel like a slog instead of a pleasant experience. This happens when you don’t take the time to understand the other person, don’t make an attempt to find out what matters to them and don’t invest in building relationships at work.

Without connecting with people, jumping to solve problems, devise solutions or collaborate on a project feels annoying, difficult and burdensome. You hate the experience. You don’t want it to repeat. All the drama and negative emotions widen the gap instead of bringing you closer to people.

The stronger are your work relationships, the easier it is to connect, collaborate and achieve goals. Relationships, built up over time, is the essential ingredient to be influential at work. People are more likely to engage with you when they feel a positive connection built using shared values, trust and mutual respect. They are more likely to value your opinions and follow your lead. They are more likely to advocate for your work and amplify your influence in meetings and decision-making processes.

In today's fast-paced world, it is tempting to look for shortcuts. But there are no quick paths to achieving lasting fame or fortune. The only sure way to success is to develop and nurture solid relationships that are grounded in trust.

Here are some of the practices I have used over the years to build real relationships at work:

If you try to fake interest or manipulate people into believing you’re genuinely interested in their work, you may get their attention for a while, but it won’t lead to a lasting connection. Putting on an act of care, warmth and empathy makes others feel tricked, exploited and deceived. Acting brave when you’re scared inside, portraying an image of an expert when you know nothing about the topic or showing your approval when you disagree with something makes you come across as insecure, insincere and phony.

Real relationships are built on a sense of connection that only shows up when you’re your most authentic self. When you don’t put on an act of perfection and embrace your vulnerability. When you’re willing to acknowledge gaps in your knowledge and show curiosity to learn from others. When you care less about building an image and more about understanding others.

Deception tactics only lead to fake relationships. Real relationships are built using trust. Manipulating others to like you, respect you or even trust you is short-lived. Others can eventually make out if you were genuine or just faking it.

Building relationships is not about transactions—it’s about connections. When we come from an authentic, genuine place in ourselves, our efforts to connect with people work to their fullest. Our relationships develop more easily and last longer, and we feel better about the people.

Don’t try to fake anything. Authenticity goes a long way in building real connections.

If you try to over-accommodate, suppress your own needs and say yes to others only to gain their approval, be liked and accepted, you may appear charming in the short-term, but always being compliant, flexible and co-operative makes you come across as a person with low confidence and low self-esteem. Your lack of honesty, tendency to overcommit and sugarcoat a problem instead of addressing it directly can lead to blind spots, missed deadlines and make problems linger on. Your reluctance to give honest feedback when it’s needed the most can lead to missed opportunities.

Real relationships are built when you speak your truth, even if it displeases someone or makes them mad. When you’re not trying very hard to appear agreeable, you end up being more helpful. When you offer honest feedback without fear of judgment, you come across as bold and confident. When you set boundaries on what’s acceptable and what’s not, you build respect by showing up as someone who knows what they want.

People pleasing only leads to hollow connections. Real relationships are built using autonomy. Putting on a facade of false harmony causes the relationship to break down and crumble under pressure.

You will never gain anyone's approval by begging for it. When you stand confident in your own worth, respect follows.

Don’t appear agreeable to be liked. Build long-lasting relationships by prioritizing assertiveness over seeking approval.

If you don’t hold others in high regard, recognize them for their work, praise and appreciate them when they do great work, you may come across as arrogant, self-centered and emotionally distant. Not elevating others with the worry that it will jeopardize your own position, make your achievements seem less significant or steal your spotlight prevents you from connecting with them at a deeper level.

Real relationships are built by making others feel important—speaking positively about them, inviting them to share their expertise or making them feel heard and understood by actively listening to them. We naturally gravitate towards people who uplift us. So, making others feel valued is a strategic way to strengthen relationships, increase your influence and come across as a supportive colleague. But it’s important that your appreciation comes across as genuine, not forced. Others can easily sense when you are complimenting them to earn a favor or trying to manipulate them to see things your way. Fake interactions can leave others feeling used which can make you come across as inauthentic, opportunist or dishonest—someone who can’t be trusted or taken seriously.

Next to physical survival, the greatest need of a human being is psychological survival—to be understood, to be affirmed, to be validated, to be appreciated. When you listen with empathy to another person, you give that person psychological air. And after that vital need is met, you can then focus on influencing or problem solving. This need for psychological air impacts communication in every area of life.

Put your ego aside. Create meaningful connections by demonstrating intellectual curiosity and showing interest in others and their work.

If you always portray an image of strength, you may hide your mistakes or try to cover up your weaknesses. Coming across as a person without flaws makes you appear cold and inhuman. Other humans, being inherently flawed, find it hard to relate to you. Not being able to see the “real you” behind that facade of perfectionism prevents others from finding a common link that will connect them to you. Using strength as a protective shield can also invoke feelings of unworthiness, inadequacy and self-doubt in others—they may avoid you to save themselves from those negative emotions.

Real relationships are built by being vulnerable—showing up as a person who’s afraid just like others, someone who doesn’t know everything, who is not always showing up as a symbol of excellence. Sharing your mistakes, acknowledging your failures and openly talking about your weaknesses not only engages others, it encourages them to be vulnerable too. It unlocks conversations that are based on honesty, sense of belonging, acceptance and inclusion. It creates a feeling of shared identity and emotional connection.

Vulnerability is not weakness, and the uncertainty, risk, and emotional exposure we face every day are not optional. Our only choice is a question of engagement. Our willingness to own and engage with our vulnerability determines the depth of our courage and the clarity of our purpose; the level to which we protect ourselves from being vulnerable is a measure of our fear and disconnection.

Stop hiding your weakness. Your flaws are what builds relationships by bringing you close to others.

If you have the habit of jumping to conclusions, blaming others or assuming bad intent when others act in ways that do not match your interest or when things don’t work out the way you expected, you may show up in ways that come across as opinionated and judgmental. Refusing to look beyond your personal narrative and evaluate the situation from another person’s perspective makes you attribute behavior to malice, bad character or incompetence. Your judgmental attitude puts others off and strains relationships—no one likes being victimized, judged and criticized. No one likes getting a “poor” character certificate.

Real relationships are built by validating assumptions, showing curiosity to understand others and exploring alternative perspectives. It requires not labeling others as “lazy, boring, incompetent, stupid, irritating, biased, reckless or rude” and instead giving them a chance and getting to know who they really are. When you make an attempt to listen with curiosity, you show your intent to understand others. Feeling heard and understood is what builds great relationships.

It's not at all hard to understand a person; it's only hard to listen without bias.

Don’t be quick to judge others. Asking what happened gets you closer to understanding, which connects people and strengthens relationships.

If you tend to put your own interests ahead of other people’s needs, you may evaluate every situation based on how it benefits you. Will sharing knowledge increase your visibility? Will solving other people’s problems earn you credit? Will attending an office party lead to better connections with the higher-ups? When your interest and participation is only based on what you’ll gain and what you have to lose, anything that involves a lose-win situation is out of scope. Anything that involves a sacrifice without getting anything in return is a big “no-no.” Anything that does not make you look better or supreme compared to others is of no value. You try to give based on what you can get. This keeps your relationships superficial and need based.

Real relationships are built by putting other people’s needs ahead of your own. Sharing your knowledge and experience without boasting, helping those in need without expecting anything in return or mentoring others without any recognition makes you come across as a genuine person who actually cares about others. Your “giving” attitude plays a big role in the love, support and respect you gain. Giving does not mean sacrificing to the level of personal harm or always putting others ahead of your own needs. It means not evaluating every situation through the lens of gain and loss, not trying to turn every situation to your advantage and not making a big deal out of every contribution.

Success depends heavily on how we approach our interactions with other people. Every time we interact with another person at work, we have a choice to make: do we try to claim as much value as we can, or contribute value without worrying about what we receive in return?

Don’t treat others as your points of leverage. Bond with others by lifting them up and trying to give more than what you take.

If you keep your interactions limited to work—bug to fix, feature to build, tasks to complete, design to review, projects to deliver—your conversations feel emotionless and transactional. Without emotions, people feel detached, disconnected and indifferent. They forget about you as soon as the work is done. Without making an attempt to know others beyond work, you fail to find a common link—like a shared interest, similar life experiences, cultural similarities or even alignment on personal philosophy—which keeps your relationships superficial without establishing a deeper connection.

Real relationships are built by taking an interest in others beyond work—showing curiosity to know about their background, their family, their schooling, their likes, dislikes and their personal goals. When you take a moment to understand the human behind work, you create the opportunity to make them feel seen and heard. It creates an instant connection that no amount of work can do. Knowing others' background, history and experience also puts you in a unique position to show empathy and compassion.

Perhaps to really know another person, you have to have a glimmer of how they experience the world.

Don’t make communication transactional. Build strong relationships by opening up, sharing your history and inviting others to share it too.

A Guide on Articulating Your Contributions as a Senior Leader

#9797. Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.

Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

#9796. nemotron-halloween

TL;DR: MonsterHouse is an interactive projection I created for Halloween. He listens to trick-or-treaters, answers in the voice of a grumpy old pirate ship and softens when visitors remember their manners. He is built on the NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent with NVIDIA Nemotron ASR, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, Magpie TTS Zeroshot and Audio2Face-3D, and he runs on a single workstation.

I wanted the kids visiting my house at Halloween to interact in a fun and unique way. The house was going to be in charge and giving out the treats, but more grumpy than scary. Somehow, my solution was to give the garage door a mouth and teach him to complain.

That became MonsterHouse: a grumpy old building with pirate stories, a fiery grin and a suspicious weakness for “please.” NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent supplies the conversation foundation. Nemotron Speech does the listening, Bolt E4B is the brain, NVIDIA Magpie TTS Zeroshot is the live voice, and NVIDIA Audio2Face-3D makes the wooden mouth talk.

The mouth came first. I imagined the wooden garage door boards splitting into jagged lips, with the burning flames of hell illuminating the driveway from beyond whenever he opened his cursed mouth. He needed to look ancient, expressive and mildly offended by the existence of visitors.

A few expressions from a house with plenty to say.

Creating a custom animation rig was one of the more labor intensive parts of the build. After bashing it into submission, I could export the facial expression shapes that Audio2Face-3D could later animate. The character SkelMesh was built in Autodesk Maya then exported into Unreal Engine where virtual fire and effects were added behind the door. With no eyes, no eyebrows and no blinking, he’s a surprisingly economical monster.

While all the nonsense of building the character was going on, NVIDIA built the Nemotron Voice Agent. What was supposed to be the hard part of the build now became rather fun, iterative and easy. I had a foundation for listening, conversation and speech right out of the box. The house already had a mouth. Now he could finally find something to complain about.

The house needed a past as cantankerous as its personality so I devised a backstory that the house had been built from the timbers of a sunken pirate ship, haunted by its stormy past. The nautical complaints now had a reason. This was the ship, reincarnated as real estate and not entirely pleased about it.

The performance needed a guide, a path to follow from greeting to goodbye while providing treats along the way. First, the house would brush visitors off with remarks like “I’m busy grumbling, go bother the neighbors!” But persistence would wear him down. A “Please” could break through immediately, and “thank you” earned a warm farewell. Once a visitor won him over, I wanted him to stay won over. Nobody wants to negotiate with the same garage door twice.

Here is where the Voice Agent really shines. You can choose any LLM you like. Because I wanted the system to be off-grid and completely self-contained, I had a memory and compute budget.

The character needs more than a prompt that says “be grumpy.” It had to follow a master conversation flow, respond to what visitors actually said, track encounter state, and leave enough compute for the rest of the pipeline.

After testing more than a dozen models, I landed on Bolt E4B to supply the live dialogue. It is an open small language model purpose-built for local conversational agents and interactive characters, which is a fair description of a talking garage door. I use the 4-bit quantized release (the “4GB” in its name) as the default response model, with the BF16 checkpoint available for comparison.

If it’s not obvious by now, I work at NVIDIA and due to this I was able to test Bolt E4B before its public release and found it to be a solid choice, with a smaller footprint than other frontrunners- Qwen3 30B-A3B and Qwen 3.6 35B-A3B.

It works inside the Nemotron Voice Agent pipeline, turning what visitors say into the next suitably reluctant reply.

Bolt provides the conversational foundation. My prompts, application logic and LoRA adapter trained on thousands of reviewed example conversations shape it into this particular stubborn ship.

Creating a dataset of over 5000 multi-turn conversations meant I could train LoRAs for each model I felt good enough to be an option. Some took about an hour to train, some took a couple. A local agent ran everything and benchmarked the results. That agent and a very large LLM created and judged the dataset to begin with. This happened at night or while I was doing the day job.

With the LoRA in place I check the replies for continuity, timing and tone, benchmark models and adapters for quality, repetition and speed, and then listen to the performance. The house should give in eventually, without turning into a cheerful concierge. A little resistance is part of the charm. An endless argument with a garage door is not.

Two shortcuts, two outputs. Authored text skips fresh dialogue generation, and saved audio skips synthesis. Clean speech drives the animation separately from the audience effects.

A haunted house loses authority if he takes too long to complain. The pipeline releases speakable text before an entire answer is finished, so the house can start talking while the rest of the sentence is still on its way. Prepared greetings and candy jokes cover familiar encounters: the text bank saves language-model work, and cached recordings save speech synthesis. Even an ancient grump benefits from rehearsing.

NVIDIA Magpie TTS Zeroshot turns text into the Queen’s English. Its zero-shot voice conditioning uses a short reference sample instead of a trained voice; mine supplies the grumpy pirate character. The house has seven moods, from grumpy and menacing to amused and delighted, and emotion tags dictated by the prompt template and provided by the LLM choose how each line is delivered. Since each emotion requires a different 3-10 second voice sample I added a “Sample your Voice” block on the UI’s tool tab. I could then read and record a sample line of text in my best happy pirate or angry pirate voice. When it’s “Go” time, Bolt E4B decides what to say, and Magpie turns that text into speech with the proper delight or despair.

Next down the pipe is Audio2Face-3D and the 3d character scene I created in Epic’s Unreal Engine. The default model weights work best with a clean neutral male or female voice, not too deep, not too high (choose the appropriate gendered model for your use case). I wanted the house to have a very deep and demonic voice with echo and chamber. In this case, since my voice samples don’t have that theatrical heft, it’s actually a benefit. Audio2Face-3D gets clean speech from the samples and a second audio stream adds adjustable real-time vocal effects that play out the speakers.

To keep everything running smoothly, I split the work to a pair of GPUs: the language and voice model pipeline runs on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q, and Unreal Engine graphics with Audio2Face-3D runs on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 4000 Blackwell. Memory isn’t the issue, compute is. I want to keep animation at a consistent frame rate regardless of what processing the agent pipeline is doing.

Voice, animation and effects have to land together. A convincing monster needs more than a fast answer; it needs to sound as though the complaint belongs to the building. In my case, he does. Tweaks to sync audio delivery are available. I’ve found I could set them and forget them. (100ms compensates for the Audio2Face-3D buffering)

Somewhere along the way, “make the house talk” required an interface full of controls. I can audition cached lines, adjust the opening mood, follow the conversation, change the voice treatment and tune the mouth animation. Tabs cover conversations, model selection, recordings, prompts, performance monitoring and camera feeds, and a soundboard and custom dialogue field let me put words in his mouth. There are also model-loading controls and an Unreal Engine connection indicator, because sometimes the monster is not sulking. He is disconnected.

The MonsterHouse control desk, with the soundboard, custom lines, opening mood and conversation flow.

The fire and glow have joined the act. Editable rules tie visual cues to delivery: live cues begin with speech, while recorded performances can follow a saved timeline. I can direct a change of mood without rebuilding the scene.

Live mode runs the trick-or-treat character. Demo mode persuades The house to explain himself. Microphone mode lets me speak through the house directly, bypassing recognition, dialogue generation and speech synthesis. My clean voice drives the mouth; the audience hears the treated version. The house considers this possession. I consider it a useful fallback.

NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni is a VLM that gives the house visual context. As an optional observer, it interprets camera images and describes visible costumes so the character has something specific to react to. Not looking to reinvent every wheel, I chose the popular object detection and tracking models YOLO and ByteTrack to count and track people currently in view. Keeping those jobs separate lets the house notice a group without asking Omni to narrate every frame.

For a suitably ridiculous test, I gave Omni a video of five costumed sheep at the door. Its saved analysis identified the pirate, vampire, witch, pumpkin and ghost outfits. That is the sort of visual context I want the house to use. Apparently even livestock have more elaborate Halloween plans than I do.

Five very woolly trick-or-treaters in a synthetic test replay. Costume labels come from the saved Omni analysis; boxes and track IDs are illustrative.

The sheep are a synthetic test, not evidence of a successful Halloween night. Real driveway groups, costumes and night lighting still need testing. Detection does trigger automatic greetings, but I fear trendy costume identification and suitably witty retorts may need some post training. Since the house has no eyes, he calls his visitor awareness echolocation. I am letting him have that one.

There is more to do: the animation can always improve, complete performance testing needs real visitors, and candy will one day be provided automatically. I have not yet reached the original goal of leaving him to run Halloween while I head off with my family to see the other neighborhood ghouls. But that is still the point of all this. One day a child will meet a grumpy old house, try a little kindness and discover that the old timber has a soft spot. And gives out candy bars.

The MonsterHouse code itself is not packaged for release, but every NVIDIA model it uses is available today, and the NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent gets you most of the way. This is the path I would follow.

A cached response bank and saved audio for your most common lines will make even a slow monster feel quick. In fact, if you happen to be limited by computing power, there is no reason why you can’t have a Live version that just uses Nemotron 3 ASR, a python conversation router, with all cached audio. You can use the Bolt E4B and Magpie pipeline to generate 100s of responses offline, then use the cache for the show. I’ll be doing this for the interactive pumpkins.

#9795. How I Built a Shared AI Memory System Using Markdown and GitHub

I’m Geoff Cox, a hands-on engineering leader in Seattle. I lead engineering teams, and I still write code.

I’m Geoff Cox, a hands-on engineering leader in Seattle. I lead engineering teams, and I still write code.

I’m Geoff Cox, a hands-on engineering leader in Seattle. I lead engineering teams, and I still write code.

For a while, every new AI session started with me re-explaining things: who I am, what I’m working on and which documents matter, often by uploading the same PDFs again. Now any AI I use starts with all of that.

This is a story about how I moved my notes out of Google Drive and into a folder of plain text files that every AI I use can read and update, and about the handful of rules that keep that folder from turning into a mess. I call it my memex.

If you read my last post, you’ve already met it. The bot that reads our kids’ school email keeps its rules there. This post is about the memex itself: what’s in it, how it stays accurate when several AIs are writing to it, and how you could start one.

In short, AIs kept tripping over my documents. When I pointed Claude at my Google Drive and asked it to edit a Google Doc, it would create a new copy instead of changing the one I had. Claude has its own documents that it can edit, but other AIs can’t easily read them. And most AIs couldn’t search my Drive well enough to find things, so I often ended up exporting documents to PDF and uploading them by hand.

I wanted one place that any AI could read, search and change, without me copying things around. A note-taking app wasn’t the answer either, since you’re limited to the structure and features the app gives you.

The name comes from Vannevar Bush’s 1945 essay “As We May Think”, where a memex is a desk that stores a person’s books, records and communications so they can be consulted quickly. Mine is a git repo of markdown files. Markdown is plain text with a little formatting, e.g. a # in front of a heading. A git repo is a folder that records every change, so you can see what changed, when and why, and undo any of it. Mine lives on my laptop and in a private repo on GitHub.

The files are organized by what they’re about:

I created the repo on March 1, 2026 from a template and then mostly forgot about it. The real work started on October 13, 2026. As of October 31, it has 131 notes and about 157,000 words.

On October 13, I downloaded my Google Drive to my laptop and had Claude read it. It extracted the text from about 780 files: PDFs, Word documents, slide decks, spreadsheets and plain text. Google Docs were the one snag. They sync to a laptop as pointer files with no text in them, so I downloaded those folders again as Word and Excel files. Claude then read the converted files too and summarized everything it had read into notes, mostly about my career and past projects, rather than copying the documents in.

Some things I didn’t want in the memex at all, so before anything was summarized we agreed on what to leave out: tax and financial records, anything that looked like it held a password, medical and identity documents, and the folders about our kids. The memex keeps a ledger of the import that lists what was read, what was skipped and why. That way a later session doesn’t redo the work, or worse, import something I had already decided to exclude.

The import surfaced something I hadn’t expected. When you read 25 years of someone’s documents side by side, they disagree with each other. For example, one of my old self-reviews said our hotfixes had dropped from 8 a week to 1.5, while my other records said 7. Rather than pick one, Claude listed every conflict like that and asked me. I answered them in batches that day, and each answer became an entry in a decisions log.

A pile of notes that several AIs write to will drift. One session restates a fact a little differently, another copies an old number from a document, and a month later nobody knows which version is right. So the memex has a few rules, and a program checks most of them on every change.

An example header. The index is built from these lines.

None of this is clever. The rules are simple enough that any AI can follow them, and the checker catches it when one doesn’t.

The checker can tell you a link is broken, but it can’t tell you that two notes say the same thing in different words, or that a plan from three weeks ago is stale. For that, there is a cleanup pass called a “dream”, loosely after the way sleep is thought to consolidate memories.

I didn’t come up with the idea. Anthropic added dreaming to Claude Managed Agents in May 2026: a scheduled process that reviews an agent’s past sessions and memory, pulls out patterns and tidies the memory, either on its own or with you reviewing the changes first. Their Code with Claude talk, “Memory and dreaming for self-learning agents”, covers how they got there. OpenClaw has its own version that runs in light, REM and deep phases and writes a diary of what it changed, and Hermes Agent has a community plugin modeled on OpenClaw’s. Mine borrows from all of them. The difference is that my memory is a git repo, so a dream’s changes arrive as a pull request I can read.

A dream has two halves. The mechanical half runs the checker and rebuilds the index. The reflective half is an AI working through a written checklist: promote anything durable from the daily log into the right note, find facts stated in more than one place and keep one owner for each, flag notes that have gone stale, and write down the questions only I can answer. It lands as a pull request with a short report.

What the AI is allowed to do on its own depends on the change:

There have been four dreams so far: October 13, October 15, October 25 and November 1. The last two were run by a bot on its own weekly schedule. On October 25, lint was already clean, so the main results were notes for the two people mentioned most often who didn’t have one yet (notes on people are private and stay in the memex), and one place where the repo’s instructions contradicted a newer decision. The November 1 dream was lighter: one lint warning fixed, the bot’s own log brought up to date and no questions for me.

More than one AI, which was the whole idea. From October 13 to 31, the memex had 190 commits and 122 merged pull requests. Most came from Claude Code sessions on my laptop. Others came from Grok Bot, the agent I use to run bots on a cloud computer, and from the bots themselves, e.g. the school bot updating its profile and a memex bot that does the weekly upkeep.

Two things fall out of that. First, I’m not tied to any one AI. If I switch tools tomorrow, the notes, the rules and the history come with me, because they’re just files. Second, every session starts with context. I don’t paste my background into a prompt or explain how something works, because the AI reads the index and finds it.

In practice, I start most things with that same memex bot. When I want to add to something or work on it, like a new project idea, a blog post I should write or a book I should read, I ask the memex bot to add the details. It already has the context of many things in my life, both current and old. And when I’m working in another AI and I think my memex would help, I give that AI read and write access to the memex’s GitHub repo, and it has the same context right away. A bot gets its own access token that works only on that one repo, can only read and write files and open pull requests, and expires within 90 days.

Pull requests turned out to be useful for more than catching an AI’s mistakes. When I want feedback on a document, I open it as a pull request and leave comments on specific lines in GitHub, the way you’d review code. The AI answers each comment and pushes a new version. This post was reviewed that way.

I think it’s relatively safe, as long as you don’t have a lot of automations that send out or post content unattended. The only bot of mine that emails anyone sends to one family list, from its own account; the others open pull requests or message me in a private Slack channel. That said, there are risks, and you certainly don’t want to store anything sensitive in your memex, e.g. credit card numbers. The checker flags anything that looks like a password or an access key, but it can’t catch everything, so the better habit is to leave those things out in the first place.

Not much, and I wouldn’t try to design it all up front. Everyone’s preferences differ, and mine weren’t clear until I’d used it for a while. A memex changes shape as you use it, and the goal is that over time it holds all of your context and preferences, written down.

That said, three things would have saved me some cleanup:

You don’t need my scripts to get most of the benefit. A folder of markdown files in a git repo, a short header on every note and an AI that can read files will get you a long way. I’d add the rest in roughly the order it paid off for me:

If you’d like a head start, I’ve put the memex’s structure and tooling on GitHub as a template, with none of my notes in it: memex-template. It has the folders, the note header, the index builder, the checker, a decisions log with an example rule, and the dream protocol with its /dream command. The bot template from my last post lives there too, since the bots deliver into the memex.

How an AI Bot Turned 30 School Emails a Week Into One Daily Digest

I’m Geoff Cox, a hands-on engineering leader in Seattle. I lead engineering teams, and I still write code.

#9794. Canva Review 2022: Details, Pricing & Features


Are you looking for a new graphic design tool? Would you like to read a detailed review of Canva? As it's one of the tools I love using. I am also writing my first ebook using canva and publish it soon on my site you can download it is free.  Let's start the review.

Canva has a web version and also a mobile app

What is Canva?

Canva is a free graphic design web application that allows you to create invitations, business cards, flyers, lesson plans, banners, and more using professionally designed templates. You can upload your own photos from your computer or from Google Drive, and add them to Canva's templates using a simple drag-and-drop interface. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop that doesn't require Graphic designing knowledge to use. It’s best for nongraphic designers.

Who is Canva best suited for?

Canva is a great tool for small business owners, online entrepreneurs, and marketers who don’t have the time and want to edit quickly.

To create sophisticated graphics, a tool such as Photoshop can is ideal. To use it, you’ll need to learn its hundreds of features, get familiar with the software, and it’s best to have a good background in design, too.

Also running the latest version of Photoshop you need a high-end computer.

So here  Canva takes place, with Canva you can do all that with drag-and-drop feature. It’s also easier to use and free. Also an even-more-affordable paid version is available for $12.95 per month.

Free vs Pro vs Enterprise Pricing plan

The product is available in three plans: Free, Pro ($12.99/month per user or  $119.99/year for up to 5 people), and Enterprise ($30 per user per month, minimum 25 people).

Free plan Features

  • 250,000+ free templates
  • 100+ design types (social media posts, presentations, letters, and more)
  • Hundreds of thousands of free photos and graphics
  • Invite members to your team
  • Collaborate and comment in real-time
  • 5GB of cloud storage
  • Try Canva Pro for free for 30 days

Pro Plan Features 

  • Everything Free, has plus:
  • 100+ million premium and  stock photos, videos, audio, and graphics
  • 610,000+ premium and free templates with new designs daily
  • Access to Background Remover and Magic Resize
  •  Create a library of your brand or campaign's colors, logos, and fonts with up to 100 Brand Kits
  • Remove image backgrounds instantly with background remover
  • Resize designs infinitely with Magic Resize
  • Save designs as templates for your team to use
  • 100GB of cloud storage
  • Schedule social media content to 8 platforms

Enterprise Plan Features

  • Everything Pro has plus:
  • Establish your brand's visual identity with logos, colors and fonts across multiple Brand Kits
  • Control your team's access to apps, graphics, logos, colors and fonts with brand controls
  • Built-in workflows to get approval on your designs
  • Set which elements your team can edit and stay on brand with template locking
  • Unlimited Storage
  • Log in with single-sign on (SSO) and have access to 24/7 Enterprise-level support.

How to Use Canva?

To get started on Canva, you will need to create an account by providing your email address, Google, Facebook or Apple credentials. You will then choose your account type between student, teacher, small business, large company, non-profit, or personal. Based on your choice of account type, templates will be recommended to you.

You can sign up for a free trial of Canva Pro, or you can start with the free version to get a sense of whether it’s the right graphic design tool for your needs.

Canva Sign Up

Designing with Canva



When you sign up for an account, Canva will suggest different post types to choose from. Based on the type of account you set up  you'll be able to see templates categorized by the following categories: social media posts, documents, presentations, marketing, events, ads, launch your business, build your online brand, etc.

 Start by choosing a template for your post or searching for something more specific. Search by social network name to see a list of post types on each network.

Templates



Next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.

You can start your design by choosing from a variety of ready-made templates, searching for a template matching your needs, or working with a blank template.


 Canva has a lot to choose from, so start with a specific search.if you want to create business card just search for it and you will see alot of templates to choose from

Elements

Inside the Canva designer, the Elements tab gives you access to lines and shapes, graphics, photos, videos, audio, charts, photo frames, and photo grids.The search box on the Elements tab lets you search everything on Canva.


To begin with, Canva has a large library of elements to choose from. To find them, be specific in your search query. You may also want to search in the following tabs to see various elements separately:

Photos

The Photos tab lets you search for and choose from millions of professional stock photos for your templates.

You can replace the photos in our templates to create a new look. This can also make the template more suited to your industry.

You can find photos on other stock photography sites like pexel, pixabay and many more or simply upload your own photos.


When you choose an image, Canva’s photo editing features let you adjust the photo’s settings (brightness, contrast, saturation, etc.), crop, or animate it.

 When you subscribe to Canva Pro, you get access to a number of premium features, including the Background Remover. This feature allows you to remove the background from any stock photo in  library or any image you upload.

Text

The Text tab lets you add headings, normal text, and graphical text to your design.

When you click on  text, you'll see options to adjust the font, font size, color, format, spacing, and text effects (like shadows). 

Canva Pro subscribers can choose from a large library of fonts on the Brand Kit or the Styles tab. Enterprise-level controls ensure that visual content remains on-brand, no matter how many people are working on it.

Audio

Create an animated image or video by adding audio to capture user’s attention in social news feeds.

If you want to use audio from another stock site or your own audio tracks, you can upload them in the Uploads tab or from the more option.

Video

Want to create your own videos? Choose from thousands of stock video clips. You’ll find videos that range upto 2 minutes

You can upload your own videos as well as videos from other stock sites in the Uploads tab. 

Once you have chosen a video, you can use the editing features in Canva to trim the video, flip it, and adjust its transparency.

Backgrounds

On the Background tab, you’ll find free stock photos to serve as backgrounds on your designs. Change out the background on a template to give it a more personal touch.

Styles


The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.

Logos

If you have a Canva Pro subscription, you’ll have a Logos tab. Here, you can upload variations of your brand logo to use throughout your designs.

With Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.

Publishing with Canva

With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

Canva Pro subscribers can create multiple post formats from one design. For example, you can start by designing an Instagram post, and Canva's Magic Resizer can resize it for other networks, Stories, Reels, and other formats.

Canva Pro subscribers can also use Canva’s Content Planner to post content on eight different accounts on Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack, and Tumblr.

Canva Team

Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

Canva Print

When it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts. 

Canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.

Canva Apps

The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

Canva Pros and Cons

Pros:

  • A user-friendly interface
  • Canva is a great tool for people who want to create professional graphics but don’t have graphic design skills.
  • Hundreds of templates, so you'll never have to start from scratch.
  • Wide variety of templates to fit multiple uses
  • Branding kits to keep your team consistent with the brand colors and fonts
  • Creating visual content on the go
  • You can find royalty free images, audio, and video without having to subscribe to another service.

Cons:

  • Some professional templates are available for Pro user only
  • Advanced photo editing features like blurring or erasing a specific area are missing.
  • Some elements that fall outside of a design are tricky to retrieve.
  • Features (like Canva presentations) could use some improvement.
  • If you are a regular user of Adobe products, you might find Canva's features limited.
  • Prefers to work with vectors. Especially logos.
  • Expensive enterprise pricing

Conclusion

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. If you have any queries let me know in the comments section.

#9793. Transformers Model Integration Contracts

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

#9792. How Surplus Is Created in a Zero-Sum Universe

Brains, People & Computers. Writes @ crive.substack.com

Brains, People & Computers. Writes @ crive.substack.com

Brains, People & Computers. Writes @ crive.substack.com

The same lines of code run on a billion phones. A twenty-six-letter alphabet can generate every sentence anyone will ever write. An explanation outlives its author and reaches stars he never saw. Knowledge compounds, finite means generate infinite ends. David Deutsch, Naval Ravikant and Brett Hall will tell you the future is open, with a straight face, and they’re right.

“All markets are zero sum. Because the universe is zero sum. There is a fixed amount of energy in the universe. Matter cannot be created nor destroyed. All so-called ‘positive sum’ games are just zero sum ones where the loser doesn’t matter.”

Both sides are true. The dissonance is not a paradox to be lived with. It is the exact condition under which surplus can be created.

This essay examines and resolves the dissonance.

The resolution determines outcomes in people, markets, products, habits and systems.

You already know some of this by instinct because it is too ubiquitous. This essay compresses it into a rule you can state — hand to someone else and apply in a domain you’ve never worked in.

Let’s start with what the optimists miss.

Bugs getting genocided by pesticides don’t matter. Bacteria getting genocided by antibiotics don’t matter. Mountains getting blown into bits and turned into highways don’t matter. Iron getting ripped from its home and melted into steel doesn’t matter. The dirt that would have been heated by the sun that is now freezing because you placed a solar panel above it doesn’t matter. Because these things aren’t sentient beings who “deserve rights” or whatever. We see no “cost” because we are not impacted by it and it doesn’t trigger our empathy response.

But there is a cost, just not to “us”. Newton’s Third Law: “every action has an equal and opposite reaction”. You cannot delete the reaction. You can only try to make that reaction occur as far away and to the least “important” possible matter as you can.

This is what economic externalities are. Trying to push that “cost” off to someone or something else. It’s not a problem when you build solar panels and steal photons from the dirt that wasn’t “using” it anyway. But the whole bug genocide thing is not so clear cut. We thought the costs went elsewhere but they did not (the bee crisis and endocrine disruption just two well-known ways in which this “costless” benefit is costing us). Same with the bacteria. And obviously there are the popular ones like CO2, pollution, or plastic filling the oceans (which are also endocrine disrupting), and plenty of others.

“Market failures” occur when the “reaction” isn’t far away enough; when the external costs aren’t external enough. Far enough to not be impacting the producer, but not so far they don’t eventually come around and bite us in the ass later.

A cost can be moved. It cannot be deleted. Everything below follows from that, one step at a time.

1. Nothing is free. Every arrangement that exists right now is having its costs paid by something, right now.

2. An arrangement is a particular order of parts. Your body is molecules in an order. A company is people and capital in an order. A city is matter in an order.

3. For any arrangement, the ways it could come apart vastly outnumber the one way it holds together. Leave coffee on a table and its heat spreads through the room, because spread-out states outnumber the concentrated one by a factor too large to write down. That count is Boltzmann’s entropy (1877).

4. So every arrangement drifts toward disorder unless something maintains it. Houses fall down. Bodies come apart. The maintenance costs energy, and the moment you stop paying, the count wins. Staying here isn’t a state. It’s a rate.

Your savings, your fitness, your reputation, your customer base, a friendship: every one of them is a rate. Stop paying and the count wins, quietly, long before anything visibly breaks.

5. The energy comes from a supply that isn’t growing. Every draw is one another arrangement can’t make. Add a new draw and every neighbour’s ceiling drops. Nobody gets to sit the contest out.

6. That leaves one condition: take in at least what you leak, at every moment, not on average. Meet it and you hold. Miss it and you shrink toward zero. Exceed it and you can allocate towards growth.

7. Everything you can see met the condition. There is no moment where a thing exists and then, separately, survives. To be here is to have passed, continuously, up to now.

8. So in a zero-sum system, survival is the only outcome that persists.

The arrangement isn’t the stuff. It’s the order the stuff is in.

The stuff comes and goes. Most of the matter in your body was something else a few years ago. Your company isn’t staffed by the people it had five years back, and your city isn’t the same buildings. What you point at when you say “that’s still the same thing” is the order.

Which means the order can ride on different substrate. A recipe survives the meal that used it up. A song survives the performance that ended. A language survives every speaker who dies.

But a pattern doesn’t float. It exists only in matter, so to continue past its current instance it has to be realised again, in new matter, before the old matter gives out. That realisation is a copy.

In a zero-sum world, copying is the only move that doesn’t forfeit survival. Every other strategy ends when the instance does.

About 330 billion of your cells die and are replaced every day (Sender and Milo, 2021).

Franchises, precedents, birthing children, and printing presses are the same move at a larger scale. Whatever is still here is here because something copied it before the last carrier wore out. It’s what persistence looks like when nothing persists.

If this sounds like Darwin, good. Darwin reached it from beetles and finches. This reaches it from the ledger, with no biology assumed, which is why it fits firms, languages and ideas as well as animals.

Variation. No copy is perfect. Fidelity is bounded by the medium: molecules misplace, memories drift, code has bugs. Each cell division copies a genome of about 6.4 billion letters with roughly one error per billion, so a few billion copies make errors certain. Variation isn’t something life adds. It’s what imperfect copying produces.

Selection. Variants that meet the rate persist. Variants that miss it vanish. Nobody needs to introduce a theory of selection. It is the filter from the last section, run on varied copies.

The cost wall. Copying costs matter and energy out of a pool that doesn’t grow. Every copy is a draw someone else can’t make. That seems to shut the door: if all anything can do is copy inside a fixed pool, nothing new can ever appear.

Yet you are reading this on something that did not exist in 1950. Where did it come from?

The universe has a conservation law for energy. It has one for matter. It has none for arrangement.

Silicon in a quarry and silicon in a chip are the same atoms under the same laws. One is rock. The other runs a hospital. The universe charged nothing for the difference.

That gap is free in the one sense the ledger tracks. It isn’t free to hold: the rate still applies to every chip and every company. Searching for a better order of the same parts costs no more matter than any other thought, and once it’s found, it copies at the price of the copy, not the price of the discovery.

Information is physical, so this isn’t a metaphor: erasing a single bit costs a minimum amount of heat (Landauer, 1961). A farming method found once fed ten thousand generations. A proof derived once spares everyone after it. Libraries exist because civilisations learned that copying is cheaper than rediscovering, and bet on that gap for five thousand years.

That is the whole difference between selling your hours and selling an arrangement with cheaper cost of replication. Hours are the Nth copy of a skill, so they compete down to the price of the copy. An arrangement is a discovery: it buys time before it is copied, and once built it copies at almost no cost.

Take the part of your work that is a discovery and turn it into something that can be copied, a tool, software, hardware, template, a system, a piece of writing.

An arrangement earns its keep when it does more than it costs to build and hold.

The wheel: stone shaped to move weight for a fraction of the effort of carrying it.

The antibiotic: a molecule that ends the bacterium and spares you.

That is surplus. It isn’t more stuff. It’s more things stuff can do.

So what is anything you make worth? Exactly the surplus it creates for whoever pays: the cost of their alternative minus the cost of yours, counted in hours, calories, materials, attention and risk.

A car beats walking by hours and calories. A spreadsheet beats hand calculation by days. That difference is the only thing there is to price.

Alex Hormozi’s value equation is this ledger with labels: the dream outcome is what the saved substrate buys, perceived likelihood is the chance the arrangement holds, time delay is the discount, and effort and sacrifice is the cost still sitting on the buyer.

The game never ends, because an arrangement that works is an intervention, not a “solution”. It changes the world, and the changed world has problems it didn’t have before. Agriculture fed cities. Cities needed coordination, coordination needed institutions, institutions needed record-keeping, record-keeping needed information technology, and information technology produced overload, which now needs better filters. No step is the last one. The hotel fills up and infinitely more guests arrive.

But finding is half the job. The other half is making sure what you found survives the copy.

The reason a book lights your brain up isn’t that the author pulled knowledge from the air. Learning is reconstruction, you are not downloading my knowledge into your brain. A good explanation takes the scattered bits you already carry and hands you one handle that regenerates all of them, so you can let the scattered bits go. If you have no scattered bits beforehand, you will fail to learn. Like a toddler looking at SpaceX blueprints.

You don’t need to memorise every species of beetle to understand biology. You need a finite rule that stands in for the infinite cases. That is what knowledge is: compression other people can load.

What separates a compression that survives from one that rots is whether it is hard to vary

Compression is lossy. A rule that covers many cases must be shorter than the cases it covers, and to be shorter it has to drop distinctions. Which distinctions are safe to drop? The ones that don’t change whether the rule works — and the only thing that tells you that is the causal structure underneath the rule.

Everything alive does whatever its constraints make cheapest.

A system is the same arithmetic inherited by everyone inside it, and a system can only see what it can count. Freelance platforms rank on price, rating and completed jobs. A newcomer has none, so price is the only variable left, and the work competes down to the lowest cost of living among the copies. The proxy can’t see the cost pushed outside it, so whoever pushes more out of sight wins more.

Evil, lazy, stupid or selfish. Each is a word for a cost structure you haven’t looked at.

Coordination has no payer. A set of rules that lets everyone move faster together costs money to design and enforce. The benefit spreads across everyone who uses it; the cost lands on who funds it. Unless people pay, nobody builds it, and the individual solution appears in its place.

The Lagos danfo bus only earns when it’s full. So the driver waits at the stop, so the buses bunch, so the road carries more vehicle-miles per passenger than a schedule would, and a trip that should take forty minutes takes an hour. Every driver is locally rational, but this causes collective disaster. The collective solution was never built, so the individual solution was forced. The difference lands on lungs, hours, health and so on.

That’s why Lagos is dirty and Singapore is clean. Singapore paid for the coordination and priced what the driver couldn’t see: a lane, a timetable, a fare that pays for the schedule instead of for being full. Nobody changed character. The prices changed and the behaviour followed.

This happens with market behaviours, academia, dating apps, tragedy of the commons, arms races, bad habits and a lot of other problems in your life. And it’s hard to escape because the only way out is through personal sacrifice and short term disadvantages for the collective long-term or larger-scale benefit, which the system punishes.

This gives you a test for anything you’re about to build or join. What does this make cheap, and what does it make expensive, for the people inside it? At ten thousand copies, where does the cost land, and who is counting it? Does it make the decent move the cheap move?

If the third answer is no, you’ve built an incentive, and people will follow it.

“If it were 2,000 years ago, we would be sacrificing ourselves to the sun gods to save us from El Niño.”

Imagine you are a member of a tribe from five thousand years ago. Bears keep coming to the camp. You sing, you dance, you leave meat at the tree line, you paint your faces and fast. Eventually the bears stop.

Now what? Remove one step and see whether they come back? One failed test and your family is eaten. So you keep everything. When deleting a necessary step is fatal and keeping an unnecessary one is cheap, keeping the whole bundle is the best move available to a mind that can’t afford the experiment. “Superstition” is what rationality looks like under that budget.

Whatever you can’t afford to test, you also can’t afford to look past — which means the reach of your concern is set by the slack you have left after survival, not by how good a person you are.

Two thousand years ago, nobody cared about endangered species or global warming. That wasn’t a shortage of virtue. Nobody could measure carbon, and nobody had surplus to spend on a species they would never meet.

The line moved for the same reason the ritual did.

The ancestor who couldn’t afford to test one step of the bear dance couldn’t afford to extend care past the fire either. Same budget.

Self comes first, because nobody can pay your rate before you do. Then kin, because kin carry copies of your pattern (kin selection, Hamilton, 1964). Then the tribe, because tribes that could count on each other beat tribes that couldn’t (reciprocity, Trivers, 1971). Each step outward sat where the cost of including someone was something the era could pay and the bill from excluding them was something the era could see.

Then surplus arrived: farming, writing, trade, law. Each raised what a society could afford to include, and each time the bill for leaving someone out became collectable: the stranger with a weapon, the plague that crossed the wall, the trading partner who could walk away.

Your boundary is who you make eat the cost, not what you say.

You live in the margin between what matter is and what it can do. That margin has no conservation law. Every arrangement that earns its keep is a deposit into it. Every discovery that gets copied is a withdrawal the next person doesn’t have to make. Every explanation that carries its why keeps a civilisation compounding on the same finite pile.

So build arrangements that earn their keep. Make them hard to vary. Hand them forward with their why. And before you celebrate, find out who paid.

The game has no finish line. Every arrangement that works creates problems that call for new ones. That isn’t a bug — it’s what it looks like when arrangements succeed. And the arrangements that stop working don’t disappear; they break down into raw material the next ones get built from. The castrated calf, the flint axe, the guild rule: the technique is forgotten and the material stays in play.

That’s where every surplus in history came from. It’s where yours will.

Why Status, Money, and Trust All Run on the Same Code

Brains, People & Computers. Writes @ crive.substack.com

#9791. Why does my challah have stretch marks?: How to stop your challah from tearing.

Recently, our Community Development Coordinator Kat Mayerovitch shared a very important update from the King Arthur Baking subreddit: a surprising amount of people were wondering why their challah has “stretch marks.”

If you’re not one of those people and don’t know exactly what that means, you may still be familiar with the problem: Sometimes, challah loaves come out of the oven with stretches or tears along the braided strands. It doesn’t affect the quality of the bread, but it does affect the appearance.

To address this issue, I asked our Baking School Curriculum Developer Jack Tissiere for their thoughts on this problem, and they identified two potential causes.

Challah dough rises twice: Once after it’s mixed (known as bulk fermentation) and a second time after the loaf is shaped or braided. Cutting short that second rise can lead to a challah that develops tears as it bakes. As Jack explains, “When we underproof our challah loaves (in other words, don't give them enough time to rise), the bread is still super active and energetic. When it hits the heat of the oven it expands energetically, and that sudden burst of volume before the dough sets can cause the bread to stretch or rip.”

How to fix: Give your braided challah loaf a little more time to rise before baking. Push the proof until the loaf is puffy and marshmallow-y; when you press it with a floured finger, the indent should slowly fill in, which is a sign that it’s ready to be baked. Sometimes, depending on the temperature of both your dough and your environment, this can take longer than the recipe says; trust your instincts rather than relying on the clock. If you fully proof the bread, when you put the loaf into the oven it’s less energetic, which means there isn’t as much oven spring (and subsequent tearing) while baking.

The other reason your challah may have stretch marks is because the loaves are shaped or braided too tightly. As Jack explains “When loaves are braided very tightly, they don’t have a lot of room to grow during the rising and baking process, causing stretches or tears as they expand.”

How to fix: Give your challah dough some slack when shaping: Braid loosely, allowing extra space for the dough to expand as it undergoes its final proof before baking. And for a pretty, even braid, start braiding from the middle; this video shows you how.

Ready to tackle your next braided loaf? Check out our Braided Challah recipe from The Big Book of Bread.
