#9774. I lost half a day to an n8n workflow that was "working." It never ran.

Last month I lost half a day to a workflow that was working perfectly. It just was not running.

An order-sync job on my self-hosted n8n had been switched off during an unrelated edit. No red execution. No error email. The dashboard was calm. The only reason I found it: someone asked why a downstream report looked stale.

That is the gap. Nearly every monitoring guide for n8n starts with an error workflow. An error workflow is good at one job, and only that job: it fires when an execution fails. It does nothing when an execution never starts.

This post is about that second case, the one most setups never alert on. I will show you why your error workflow is blind to it, then build a small liveness check that catches it, and I tested the whole thing on a production-shaped stack: n8n 2.43.6 on PostgreSQL 16 on an Amazon Linux 2023 EC2 box. Not the default SQLite demo. The same shape you actually run.

This is a follow-up to my earlier post on securing self-hosted n8n on AWS. If you followed that one, this plugs the monitoring hole it leaves open.

Here is n8n's own line on when an error workflow runs. It runs if an execution fails. Read that again. It needs an execution to exist before it can judge it failed.

Now think about how a scheduled workflow actually dies in production. It rarely throws. It goes quiet:

In every one of those, the trigger never fires. No execution record is created. There is no failed run for the error workflow to catch, because there is no run at all.

So the alerting you trust most is structurally incapable of seeing the most common way a cron job dies. It is not misconfigured. It is pointed at the wrong thing.

When you unpublish a workflow, n8n even tells you what happens next, in the confirmation dialog, in its own words:

This will prevent all production executions to this workflow until you publish again.

Prevent all production executions. That is the whole problem in n8n's own words, printed right there in the UI, and no error workflow is listening for it.

I did not want to take this on faith, so I ran it.

I stood up n8n 2.43.6 against PostgreSQL 16 on an EC2 instance, imported a tiny workflow called Order sync on a one-minute schedule trigger, and published it. Two scheduled runs showed up right away through the public API, both with mode: trigger and status: success.

Then I unpublished it and watched the execution list through the API.

Zero. Two and a half minutes, at least two scheduled runs missed, and the execution count did not move by one.

Look at what that execution list shows: every run before the unpublish says "Succeeded." There is no red run, no error, nothing for an error workflow to fire on. Just an absence that starts the moment the workflow goes quiet.

No execution means no status to read. No status means nothing an error workflow could fire on. I republished, and within 70 seconds a new run appeared and the count went from 2 to 3. The trigger resumed exactly where it left off, and for those 150 seconds, every internal error alert I could have wired up would have stayed silent.

That is the silent failure. Not a red run you missed. A run that never happened.

If you would rather watch it than read it, here is the same thing in 90 seconds, break it, watch nothing fire, fix it:

If waiting for a failure cannot work, the check has to invert the question. Instead of "did anything fail," it asks "did the thing I expect actually run, and is it still able to run."

A separate scheduled workflow, every 15 minutes, reads the n8n public API and answers four questions for each workflow on a watch list:

Three API calls do all of it. These are the real response shapes from my run, not docs:

The active field is the published flag. When I unpublished Order sync, active flipped to false, and that one boolean is the whole detection. No execution needed.

Two design rules make this usable instead of annoying:

Only email on change. A problem that stays open gives you one email, not one every 15 minutes. The check keeps the last state and compares. New problem opened, send once. Problem cleared, send a "back to normal." Nothing changed, stay silent. A monitor that cries every cycle gets filtered to a folder you never open, and then it is not a monitor.

Keep one check outside n8n. More on that below, because it is the part people skip and then regret.

I wrote the check as a plain Python script so this whole tutorial is free and reproducible with nothing but the n8n API. You can run it from cron, a Lambda, or wrap the same logic in an n8n workflow. Here is the core of it:

Running it against my real stack, across the three states:

That middle state is the one your error workflow never prints.

Here is the setup I actually ran. It uses a small test stack so you can prove the behaviour safely before you point it at real workflows. The one real external dependency is Mailpit, a throwaway mail server so you can see the alert without a real SMTP account.

A note on versions, because it bit me and will bite you. On n8n 2.43.6, Postgres 16 logs this on boot:

Everything in this post worked fine on 16.15. But if you are standing up a fresh box, start on Postgres 17 so you are not on compatibility-only support.

Put the docker-compose.yml from the repo in an empty folder. It runs n8n 2.43.6 on Postgres 16 and Mailpit, all bound to 127.0.0.1 only.

Expect three containers. Postgres becomes healthy, then n8n runs its migrations against it. Wait for the health check:

On a real EC2 box, do not open 5678 or 8025 in the security group. Keep them on localhost and reach them over an SSH tunnel:

Open http://localhost:5678, create the owner account. Then Settings -> n8n API -> Create API key. Give it an expiration you will actually renew (a long-lived key is one more secret to rotate; set a calendar reminder rather than "Never"). Copy it with the copy button, because n8n shows the full key only once.

One thing worth knowing that the usual guides do not test: a narrow-scoped key is enough. I ran the check with a key scoped to workflow:read, workflow:list, execution:read, execution:list and nothing else, and it worked. A key with no write scope got a clean {"message":"Forbidden"} on any write. So the monitor key cannot change anything even if it leaks. Give it read scopes only.

Import order-sync.json (in the repo). It is a schedule trigger plus a code node that returns two fake orders. It does nothing outside n8n, so it is safe to publish and break. Publish it.

Add Order sync to the watch list with a max_quiet_minutes of 10, which means "shout if there has been no successful run in 10 minutes." Run the check (or set the watch workflow to every 15 minutes). First healthy run says nothing is wrong.

Unpublish Order sync. The next check prints:

That is the alert your error workflow cannot produce. Publish it again and the next check clears to "back to normal." Then set your real interval to 15 minutes and add every workflow you care about to the WATCH list in the script.

The -v removes the Postgres, n8n, and Mailpit volumes. On your real instance you obviously keep them, and you keep the check running on 15 minutes.

Here is the uncomfortable part, and it is the reason I will not tell you this check is enough on its own.

The check runs inside n8n. If n8n itself is down, out of memory, mid-restart, or the EC2 instance is stopped, the check does not run either. A monitor that lives inside the thing it watches dies with it, with no noise, and the dashboard stays calm because there is no dashboard.

This is the single blind spot no amount of internal instrumentation closes. You need one thing outside the box.

The pattern is a heartbeat. After every check, the workflow pings an external uptime or cron-monitoring service. You tell that service to expect a ping every 15 minutes. When the pings stop, the outside service alerts you, because the absence of a ping is the signal. The workflow going quiet is exactly what you want to hear about.

I have not wired the heartbeat into my own run yet, so I am not going to pretend I measured it. I am flagging it as the required second layer, because leaving it out is how people end up with a monitor that was itself dead for a week. Treat the in-n8n check and the external heartbeat as one system, not two options.

Set max_quiet_minutes to the rhythm, not a guess. My rule: about 3x the schedule interval. Every 15 minutes gets 45. Hourly gets 130. Daily gets 1500. For event-driven workflows (webhooks with no schedule), set it to 0, so you only check "exists and published," because there is no expected rhythm to be late against.

Keep executions long enough to read. The check reads past runs from the execution list. If your pruning deletes successful runs faster than your max_quiet_minutes window, the freshness check goes blind. Set EXECUTIONS_DATA_SAVE_ON_SUCCESS: all and make sure EXECUTIONS_DATA_MAX_AGE and EXECUTIONS_DATA_PRUNE_MAX_COUNT keep runs around longer than your largest quiet window.

Cost: effectively zero. This is a few API reads every 15 minutes on a box you already pay for. The external heartbeat service has a free tier that covers a handful of monitors. There is no new infrastructure here, which is the point. Monitoring that needs its own cluster never gets installed.

What I would not do: reach for Prometheus and Grafana just for this. If you already run them, N8N_METRICS=true exposes a metrics endpoint and that is a fine path. But standing up a metrics stack to answer "did my workflow run" is a lot of moving parts to watch a boolean. Match the tool to the question.

I built this for my own n8n setup after getting bitten by exactly this blind spot, ran it on my real stack, and liked it enough to write it up. Everything here runs on the free n8n API alone, so you can take the check as-is or adapt it to your own workflows.

I did not arrive at this idea cold. I first came across the "did it run?" approach through Krafera Silent Failure Watch, a packaged monitoring pack that Ahmet at Krafera built and gave me a copy of to try. That pack is what made me sit up and realise my own setup had this exact hole, so the honest thing is to say so up front.

Full disclosure, because this article runs on trust: Ahmet gave me a copy rather than my buying it, and I am not an affiliate, I earn nothing whether you buy it or not. I am writing about it because I use it, I genuinely rate it, and it is the thing that put me onto this blind spot.

What it actually is: a set of importable n8n workflows that run on your own instance and email you in plain text, one message on a bad day, nothing on a clean one. The entry tier is the same "Did it run" check this post builds (exists, published, last run not failed, ran in time), set up out of the box the way a monitor should be: it emails once when something breaks and then stays quiet until the state changes, sends a "back to normal" when it recovers, and can ping an outside heartbeat so a stopped check or a stopped server shows up on an external monitor, the one gap my script leaves open. The higher tiers add the parts I did not build here: a daily count check that matches yesterday's orders between a source and a destination and names the missing, extra and different rows; an error alert that reports the workflow, node and failed record with secrets masked; and on the top tier, webhook de-duplication, a retry queue, nightly backups and a weekly health email. Krafera tested the pack on the same n8n version I used, 2.43.6 in Docker, on the default SQLite database rather than the Postgres-on-EC2 stack I ran, and on the n8n 3.0.1 pre-release, with the bad days made on purpose and the emails counted.

Where it earns its keep: if you would rather import a tested file than keep a script running, or you want the count-check and error-alert pieces I left out, Krafera Silent Failure Watch saves you the half a day I spent building and testing mine. For freelancers maintaining this across a handful of client instances, that is squarely the right call, one import and a Settings node instead of a script per box.

I still wrote my own open check for this post so the tutorial stays free and reproducible on the public API, and because I wanted to understand the mechanism end to end rather than just install it. Both get you to the same place for the core check. If the packaged route fits how you work, Krafera Silent Failure Watch is worth a look: Krafera Silent Failure Watch.

I am specific about this because "tested" should mean tested.

Verified on my stack (2026-10-27, UTC): n8n 2.43.6 on PostgreSQL 16.15, amd64, Amazon Linux 2023 EC2, Docker 25.0.14, Compose v2.39.1. The unpublish produces zero executions (measured over 150s). The three API shapes above. The three-state check output. A test alert delivered through SMTP to Mailpit. A read-only scoped API key working, and a write attempt correctly forbidden.

Not tested, so not claimed: the external heartbeat end to end, a real SMTP provider (I only used Mailpit), the n8n 1.x to 2.x upgrade on Postgres, queue mode, and n8n Cloud. If you run any of those, treat the relevant step as "should work, verify on your side."

That is the honest line between what I ran and what I am reasoning about.

Everything here, the compose file, the sample workflow, the standalone check, the EC2 and Postgres notes, and the architecture diagram, is in the repo:

🛰️ A follow-up to getting self-hosted n8n running on AWS: this plugs the monitoring hole that setup leaves open.

From here, the Build it step by step section above walks the whole setup: docker compose up -d, create a read-only API key, then python3 did_it_run_check.py. The README covers the same.

If this saved you a stale-report debugging session, the comment box is open (see below).

Here is the stance I will defend in the comments: most n8n monitoring advice is theatre. It tells you to build an error workflow, which watches for failures. But the failure that actually took my workflow down could not produce a failure, by definition. An alert that can only fire on a run that happened is blind to the most common way a scheduled job dies, which is a run that never happened. We keep instrumenting the thing that is easy to catch instead of the thing that actually bites.

So two questions, and I genuinely read every answer:

Disagree? Tell me where this reasoning falls down. That is the most useful comment you can leave.

Part 1 was securing self-hosted n8n on AWS: the hardening that gets the stack safely online. This post is the monitoring layer that setup leaves open, the alert for the failure that produces no failure. Harden it, then make sure you would know the day it quietly stopped. Both live in the repo.

New York, USA, November 2nd, 2026/TechnologyWire/--UseQR today announced the launch of its enhanced QR code generator platform, introducing expanded customization and functionality designed to help businesses create, manage and track their QR code-based communications.

As QR codes continue to serve as a connection between businesses and their customers, UseQR aims to build on this established technology by bringing multiple business-oriented tools together in one platform. The service allows users to generate customized QR codes for different purposes, from sharing contact information and website links to providing access to digital content and communication channels.

The platform also includes dynamic QR codes, which allow users to update linked information after a code has been printed, alongside analytics tools for monitoring scan activity.

QR code generators and scannable icons have long been fixtures in the marketing landscape. From a WiFi QR code in a hotel to a QR code for a restaurant menu, these small digital tools have become part of everyday customer interactions. For this reason, the recent launch of a marketing service focused on a custom QR code generator of a new iteration has captured everyone’s attention.

The primary advantage of such platforms remains accessibility, making them suitable for businesses of any scale, from small enterprises to large corporations. Cafes, agencies, and sellers which can utilize vCard QR codes. It's designed for anyone who has ever had to include a substantial amount of information on a business card, in a chat, or in professional correspondence.

According to John Doe, a representative of the UseQR development team, in their work, they do not set out to spark a revolution or shock the world with radical innovations. "The truth is, every business, from a small family-run bakery to a major automotive corporation, is built on the little details. This attention to detail makes the difference between success and failure. That is why we took a small cornerstone element of any enterprise and refined it to perfection."

The subject in question is a rather archaic technology that, today, serves as a primary bridge between a potential customer and a business, acting as a modern-day business card or promotional flyer. It is the QR code: a long-standing invention that, for some reason, never received the attention or development it deserved.

What else besides a QR code generator with logo

Nowadays, developers strive to create a product that, in functionality, practicality, and reliability, resembles a Swiss Army knife. After all, generating a custom icon can be done with any free online service. What truly matters is adding features and ergonomics that make it more than a QR code generator with a logo. For instance, the product UseQR goes beyond simple icon generation by offering users a range of extra options:

"Our goal was quite simple," John Doe continues. "We had a solid, existing concept and perfected it by enhancing its usability and optimizing its functionality."

Until recently, it seemed impossible to make the typically dull, uniform QR patterns aesthetically pleasing. To many average consumers, that chaotic, almost infernal arrangement of dots or squares evoked a sense of bleak, dreary monotony. Hardly the kind of thing that would inspire someone to point their phone camera at it to discover the information hidden within.

Modern market solves this problem. And not just by letting you add a logo or use a template. Clients get a full-fledged editor with a robust set of features that is simple and enjoyable to operate.

A UseQR online QR code generator is a useful, convenient tool for businesses of any size and sector, perfect for anyone who wants to present information in a concise, user-friendly format without compromising the aesthetic appeal of their message. #9772. AIO Best Practices

Posted on Nov 3 • Originally published at kevinleary.net

I took a wireless security company from invisible to the #1 recommendation across ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Perplexity for their ideal buyers, and I documented how that was done. The strategy decks making the rounds right now, including the ones venture firms are circulating to their portfolio companies, get a real portion of this right. They also get a few important things wrong, and they consistently underweight the parts that are hardest to fake. This is my version of the playbook: what the industry consensus has correct, where I break from it, and the work I believe actually compounds. I’ve also put the whole thing into a free slide deck you can reference or share with your team: view it on Google Slides or download the PowerPoint.

AEO, GEO, AIO, AI SEO: these all describe the same discipline, which is making your brand and products the thing AI systems reference when your buyers ask questions. I use AEO on this site, the agency world has largely settled on GEO, and AIO is gaining ground. Do not let anyone convince you these are different services. The label changes, the work does not.

Credit where due, because the consensus forming around a few ideas is correct. Separating conversion pages from informational content. Buyer pages should be built for people ready to act, and informational content should be built to be extracted, cited and reassembled by machines. Mixing the two produces pages that do neither job well. Query fan-out. When someone asks an AI assistant a complex question, the system decomposes it into smaller questions, retrieves answers for each piece, and reassembles them. Your content needs to address the pieces, not just the headline topic. This is the single most useful mental model to come out of the current wave of AI search thinking, and it should shape how you structure every informational page. Baseline before optimizing. Run the prompts your buyers actually use, today, across the major assistants, and record who gets recommended. Most brands have never done this and are optimizing blind. Traditional on-page fundamentals still carry the weight. Clear structure, real headings, lists and tables, parseable paragraphs. LLMs consume the same rendered content search crawlers do, and clean markup is easier to extract from than page builder soup.

The most measurably successful AI optimization work I’ve done, the projects where increased traffic could be directly attributed to AI sources, all started the same way: with research into how a language model actually trains, and how it would go about training itself by browsing a website. That exercise matters because it’s fundamentally different from how a search bot indexes. A crawler looks for expected structure: titles, headings, links, markup signals. It files pages. An LLM reads the freeform content of a page to understand it: what you know, what you do, who you serve, and whether the way you describe it hangs together. Optimizing for a filing system and optimizing for a reader are different jobs, and most SEO habits were built for the filing system. Before touching a single page, spend the time understanding the reader. Everything else on this list gets easier to prioritize once you have. Now for where I differ.

Nearly every AIO checklist in circulation includes adding an llms.txt file, and it is the one item on those lists with actual evidence against it. Google has said on the record it does not use the file. OpenAI documents robots.txt as its crawler control and never mentions llms.txt. Server log studies across thousands of domains show the major AI crawlers never request it. I laid out the full case in my post on whether AI systems read llms.txt. What I build instead is a dynamic JSON endpoint generated from the live site, like the one at /llm-api/ here. It returns structured, always-current data: services, products, specifications, case studies, FAQs with citable anchors, availability, contact methods. It can never drift out of sync because it is generated, and it hands a machine typed fields instead of prose to interpret. If you want an llms.txt for completeness, make it a pointer to that endpoint and nothing more.

The contents are discretionary, and the filter I use is simple: anything related to authority and credibility belongs in there. For a security technology client, that meant the patents associated with the founders and the underlying tech, and the government certifications the product holds for federal security standards. Facts like those are exactly what a model can verify and confidently repeat when it recommends a product. It also means full product specifications, stated precisely: the exact frequency ranges a detection product covers, the deployment requirements, the integration surface. Vague capability language gives a model nothing to work with. A number does.

The consensus is right that structured data matters and wrong about how to produce it. The common advice is to install an SEO plugin or paste AI-generated schema blocks into your pages. Both produce the same problem: generic, frequently inaccurate markup that goes stale the moment your content changes. Schema should be generated cleanly as part of your templates, from the same data that renders the page. When the content changes, the markup changes with it, automatically. That is the only way it stays truthful at scale. Most schema out there is copy-paste: an out-of-the-box plugin, or whatever markup everyone else in the industry ships. There are much better ways to describe a page or a site, and finding them requires actually researching what schema.org offers. Reviewing the vocabulary itself surfaces precise types and properties most sites never use, and the right choices are page-specific decisions based on a real understanding of the spec, not a site-wide default. Schema.org is a large vocabulary, and fluency means knowing what to use and, just as importantly, what not to use and where. Precise Organization, Product, Service, Person, FAQPage and TechArticle markup with real, verifiable properties gives a model unambiguous facts to repeat. Bolting AggregateRating onto pages without reviews, stacking irrelevant types, or marking up content that does not exist on the page does the opposite: it teaches systems your markup cannot be trusted. The goal is a machine-readable version of the truth, not a keyword stuffing exercise in JSON.

One piece of this deserves its own callout because it’s cheap, obvious in hindsight, and skipped constantly: every single social profile and third-party site associated with your business should be declared, consistently, in three places. The sameAs property of your Organization schema, your LLM data API, and linked from the site itself. LinkedIn, GitHub, YouTube, Crunchbase, G2, industry directories, review profiles, all of it. This directly builds your knowledge graph: models assemble an entity picture of a business by connecting its profiles across the web, and declaring those connections yourself means the graph gets built correctly instead of guessed at. I maintain the full set on this site in all three places, and it’s part of the standard setup for every client.

Here is the part I think matters more than anything else on any of these lists, and it barely appears on them. AI assistants let people ask far more detailed and specific questions than Google ever rewarded. Nobody typed a forty word query with three constraints into a search box, because ten blue links could not answer it. People absolutely ask assistants questions like that, and the assistant will name a specific product if, and only if, it has the detail to justify the recommendation. This is the long tail all over again, except the tail is now conversational and effectively infinite. Brands need to put absolutely every specification, technical detail, integration, limitation and use case of their products into structured, published form. The detailed compatibility matrix nobody wanted to maintain, the deployment requirements, the edge case scenarios your sales engineers answer on calls: all of it. When a model has trained on or retrieved deep product specifics, it can reference your product when the highly specific question comes, and your competitors with thin marketing pages cannot be part of that answer. A controlled experiment published at SIGIR 2026 put numbers on this. Researchers ran 252,000 trials across six language models, showing each one two otherwise identical pages that differed by exactly one characteristic, and recorded which got cited. Two of the four universal gatekeepers were stating a price and including technical specifications. Pages that omitted either lost decisively to pages that included them, across every model tested. The detail is not a nice-to-have, it is the price of entry. The flip side is a real constraint: you can’t bend the truth about what your product can do, overstate its reach, or position it for a market it doesn’t truly serve. Language models cross-reference everything you publish against everything everyone else has published, and inconsistencies surface in answers where you will never see them happen. Grounded, verifiable claims are the ones that survive into answers, and accuracy has quietly become the strongest positioning strategy there is.

LLMs do not care about keywords at all. They understand whole subject areas, and they can tell whether what you’re saying makes sense for the scenario being asked about. Making sure a phrase appears over and over, the reflex two decades of SEO trained into everyone, buys you nothing with a model. What matters now is using the precise terminology a subject calls for, in the right context. Describe what you do and what your product does as clearly as possible, with the words a knowledgeable person in your field would actually use, and stop worrying about keyword placement. Clarity is the ranking factor.

Before you publish anything new, deal with the redundant content you already have. Most established sites carry years of republished, overlapping posts that all say roughly the same thing, and that redundancy actively hurts you: authority splits across near-duplicates, and a model choosing a source to cite picks the page that answers completely rather than any fragment from your pile. Merge the overlapping pieces into one authoritative page, redirect the losers into the winner, and remove pages that exist only to exist. Then hold every surviving page to a simple standard: be clear and honest about your product. Say what it does, who it is for, and what it costs to the extent you can. Vague positioning language survives fine in a world of skimmed landing pages and dies in a world where a machine is trying to extract facts. This is what it looked like in practice for a security technology client: the same subject matter was scattered across the site in every format at once, resource pages, videos, blog posts and downloads, with no single page answering anything completely. We consolidated all of it into deep research pages, one authoritative page per subject, and those pages are what the models now cite. It measurably worked, and it’s the same consolidation play I documented in the case study.

The measurement layer being sold with AIO engagements centers on AI share of voice: your brand’s percentage of mentions across a broad basket of prompts, tracked in a dashboard, trending week over week. The industry is settling on it as the de facto performance standard, and I disagree that it’s the key metric. I’ve watched engagements where share of voice looked great and very few leads actually arrived from AI, because breadth across loosely related prompts is not what produces buyers. What every brand marketer should track instead is brand mentions for the specific prompts their buyers actually use, and repeated variants of those prompts over time. A security architect evaluating your category asks a handful of question patterns, phrased a dozen ways. Whether you are the answer for those patterns is the entire game. Whether you appear in a thousand loosely related prompts is trivia. And if you do not know the prompts your audience is searching, that is the finding: you need to double down and understand that audience better. Prompt research is customer research now. The interviews, the sales call recordings, the support tickets, the words buyers use when they describe their problem to a colleague: that is where the prompt list comes from, and no tool subscription substitutes for knowing it. I covered the click-side measurement half of this in Measuring AEO & SEO Performance.

The same core fundamentals of SEO will always apply to AIO, and the cleanest expression of them remains Google’s E-E-A-T framework: Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness and Trust. Content grounded in first-hand experience, written by identifiable people with demonstrable expertise, published by an organization with verifiable credentials, consistent facts and honest claims. That framework was designed as a description of what makes information worth surfacing, which is exactly why it transfers. An LLM deciding what to cite is running a version of the same evaluation, and every credential, patent, certification, named client and published result you can state plainly and verifiably is weight on your side of it. E-E-A-T was always a description of the destination, and it remains the ideal high-level approach no matter which acronym the industry lands on next.

A technical edge worth adding to the list: serve your pages as Markdown to the AI systems that ask for it. Same URL, two representations, using standard content negotiation: browsers get HTML, and a crawler sending Accept: text/markdown gets clean structured Markdown with no nav, scripts or layout markup, and far fewer wasted tokens. I’ve written up the full approach in serving a website as Markdown to AI bots, and this site does it live. Speed is part of the same story. Citation research from late 2025 found pages painting in under 0.4 seconds averaged 6.7 AI citations against 2.1 for pages over 1.13 seconds, because AI crawlers operate on tight compute budgets and time out fast. Expect that pressure to increase as these systems hit harder limits on what they can consume and how often. Fast, lean, already-structured responses are what get consumed, and Cloudflare’s Markdown for Agents is the best option I know for delivering them: one toggle, edge conversion, the whole site covered.

A note of caution before the close: we are in a wild west period where AIO is being chased for a great deal of money, and there are big players making confident claims based on broad generalizations rather than observed results. Nobody outside the AI labs fully knows how these systems weight sources, and the systems themselves change quarterly. When you evaluate anyone’s advice in this space, mine included, ask one question: what did you actually change, for which brand, and what happened in the answers afterward? Frameworks without receipts are marketing. The honest version of this discipline runs experiments, measures prompt-level outcomes, and holds its own theories loosely.

Strip away the acronyms and the dashboards and what remains is this: at the highest level, LLMs are seeking to do exactly what Google has sought to do for twenty five years, which is to provide people with the very best answer to their questions. They will use all available data today, and every new source of data in the future, to keep making those answers better. Every optimization tactic is downstream of that objective, and tactics that fight it have a shelf life measured in months. The long-term play is to make your brand and your products the best answer. That is the hard work that pays off, and it is genuinely hard: it involves difficult, honest answers to product questions, real marketing focus, and publishing the unglamorous detail your competitors will not bother with. Most brands will keep chasing the tactic of the quarter instead. The brands that do the work will be the brands. It really is that simple, and that unforgiving.

Supporting research: Vishwakarma, Kumar and Jamidar (2026), What Gets Cited: Competitive GEO in AI Answer Engines, SIGIR ’26, and LLM Ranking Factors 2026 from The Digital Bloom. I break both studies down in AI Ranking Factors.

#9771. ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?

ProWritingAid VS Grammarly:  When it comes to English grammar, there are two Big Players that everyone knows of: the Grammarly and ProWritingAid. but you are wondering which one to choose so here we write a detail article which will help you to choose the best one for you so Let's start

What is Grammarly?

Grammarly is a tool that checks for grammatical errors, spelling, and punctuation.it gives you comprehensive feedback on your writing. You can use this tool to proofread and edit articles, blog posts, emails, etc.

Grammarly also detects all types of mistakes, including sentence structure issues and misused words. It also gives you suggestions on style changes, punctuation, spelling, and grammar all are in real-time. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.


Features of Grammarly

  • Spelling and Word Suggestion: Grammarly detects basic to advance grammatical errors and also help you why this is an error and suggest to you how you can improve it
  • Create a Personal Dictionary: The Grammarly app allows you to add words to your personal dictionary so that the same mistake isn't highlighted every time you run Grammarly.
  • Different English Style: Check to spell for American, British, Canadian, and Australian English.
  • Plagiarism: This feature helps you detect if a text has been plagiarized by comparing it with over eight billion web pages.
  • Wordiness: This tool will help you check your writing for long and hard-to-read sentences. It also shows you how to shorten sentences so that they are more concise.
  • Passive Voice: The program also notifies users when passive voice is used too frequently in a document.
  • Punctuations: This feature flags all incorrect and missing punctuation.
  • Repetition: The tool provides recommendations for replacing the repeated word.
  • Proposition: Grammarly identifies misplaced and confused prepositions.

  • Plugins: It offers Microsoft Word, Microsoft Outlook, and Google Chrome plugins.


What is ProWritingAid?

ProWritingAid is a style and grammar checker for content creators and writers. It helps to optimize word choice, punctuation errors, and common grammar mistakes, providing detailed reports to help you improve your writing. 

ProWritingAid can be used as an add-on to WordPress, Gmail, and Google Docs. The software also offers helpful articles, videos, quizzes, and explanations to help improve your writing.

Features of ProWriting Aid

Here are some key features of ProWriting Aid:

  • Grammar checker and spell checker: This tool helps you to find all grammatical and spelling errors.
  • Find repeated words:  The tool also allows you to search for repeated words and phrases in your content.
  • Context-sensitive style suggestions:  You can find the exact style of writing you intend and suggest if it flows well in your writing.
  • Check the readability of your content: Pro Writing Aid helps you identify the strengths and weaknesses of your article by pointing out difficult sentences and paragraphs.
  • Sentence Length: It also indicates the length of your sentences.
  • Check Grammatical error: It also checks your work for any grammatical errors or typos, as well.
  • Overused words: As a writer, you might find yourself using the same word repeatedly. ProWritingAid's overused words checker helps you avoid this lazy writing mistake.
  • Consistency: Check your work for inconsistent usage of open and closed quotation marks.
  • Echoes: Check your writing for uniformly repetitive words and phrases.

Difference between Grammarly and Pro-Writing Aid

Grammarly and ProWritingAid are well-known grammar-checking software. However, if you're like most people who can't decide which to use, here are some different points that may be helpful in your decision.

Grammarly vs ProWritingAid

  • Grammarly is a writing enhancement tool that offers suggestions for grammar, vocabulary, and syntax whereas ProWritingAid offers world-class grammar and style checking, as well as advanced reports to help you strengthen your writing.
  • Grammarly provides Android and IOS apps whereas ProWritingAid doesn't have a mobile or IOS app.
  • Grammarly offers important suggestions about mistakes you've made whereas ProWritingAid  shows more suggestions than Grammarly but all recommendations are not accurate
  • Grammarly has a more friendly UI/UX whereas the ProWritingAid interface is not friendly as Grammarly.
  • Grammarly is an accurate grammar checker for non-fiction writing whereas ProWritingAid is an accurate grammar checker for fiction writers.
  • Grammarly finds grammar and punctuation mistakes, whereas ProWritingAid identifies run-on sentences and fragments.
  • Grammarly provides 24/7 support via submitting a ticket and sending emails. ProWritingAid’s support team is available via email, though the response time is approximately 48 hours.
  • Grammarly offers many features in its free plan, whereas ProWritingAid offers some basic features in the free plan.
  • Grammarly does not offer much feedback on big picture writing; ProWritingAid offers complete feedback on big picture writing.
  • Grammarly is a better option for accuracy, whereas ProWritingAid is better for handling fragmented sentences and dialogue. It can be quite useful for fiction writers.

ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Pricing Difference

  • Grammarly offers a Premium subscription for $30/month for a monthly plan  $20/month for quarterly and $12/month for an annual subscription.
  • The Business plan costs $12.50 per month for each member of your company.

ProWritingAid vs Grammarly – Pros and Cons

  • Personal dictionary

  • Allows you to make changes to a document without altering its formatting.
  • Helps users improve vocabulary
  • User-friendly interface
  • Browser extensions and MS word add-ons
  • Available on all major devices and platforms
  • Grammarly will also offer suggestions to improve your style.
  • Enhance the readability of your sentence
  • Free mobile apps 
  • Offers  free version

Grammarly Cons

  • Supports only English 
  • Customer support only via email
  • Limits to 150,000 words
  • Subscription plans can be a bit pricey 
  • Plagiarism checker is only available in a premium plan
  • Doesn’t offer a free trial
  • No refund policy
  • The free version is ideal for basic spelling and grammatical mistakes, but it does not correct advanced writing issues.

ProwritingAid Pros

  • It offers more than 20 different reports to help you improve your writing.
  • Less expensive than other grammar checkers.
  • This tool helps you strengthen your writing style as it offers big-picture feedback.
  • ProWritingAid has a life plan with no further payments required.

  • Prowritingaid works on both Windows and Mac.

ProWritingAid Cons

  • Editing can be a little more time-consuming when you add larger passages of text.
  • ProWritingAid currently offers no mobile app for Android or iOS devices.
  • Plagiarism checker is only available in premium plans.
  • All recommendations are not accurate

Summarizing the Ginger VS Grammarly: My Recommendation

As both writing assistants are great in their own way, you need to choose the one that suits you best.

  • For example, go for Grammarly  if you are a non-fiction writer
  • Go for ProWritingAid if you are a fiction writer.
  • ProWritingAid is better at catching errors found in long-form content. However, Grammarly is more suited to short blog posts and other similar tasks.
  • ProWritingAid helps you clean up your writing by checking for style, structure, and content while Grammarly focuses on grammar and punctuation.
  • Grammarly has a more friendly UI/UX whereas; ProWritingAid offers complete feedback on big picture writing.

Both ProWritingAid and Grammarly are awesome writing tools, without a doubt. but as per my experience, Grammarly is a winner here because Grammarly helps you to review and edit your content. Grammarly highlights all the mistakes in your writing within seconds of copying and pasting the content into Grammarly’s editor or using the software’s native feature in other text editors.

Not only does it identify tiny grammatical and spelling errors, it tells you when you overlook punctuations where they are needed. And, beyond its plagiarism-checking capabilities, Grammarly helps you proofread your content. Even better, the software offers a free plan that gives you access to some of its features.

#9770. How to Write Technical SEO Tickets Developers Can Implement and Test

We offer specialist SEO Services for Ecommerce Stores. Get more potential buyers to your store.

We offer specialist SEO Services for Ecommerce Stores. Get more potential buyers to your store.

We offer specialist SEO Services for Ecommerce Stores. Get more potential buyers to your store.

A technical SEO ticket should describe an observable change to a specific page or component, the evidence that will prove it, and the existing behaviour that must survive. That gives engineering a delivery target and gives the person reviewing the release a test they can actually repeat.

Improve internal linking on our product pages.

A developer could add links to a footer, introduce a recommendation widget or change a navigation component. Those are different changes. The request has left the decision about placement, behaviour and scope unfinished.

I would rather turn that request into a small release contract: an agreed change, a bounded set of preserved behaviours and a check against the public result.

For this worked example, imagine a boot retailer with a product page at /products/leather-walking-boots/ and a useful care guide at /guides/boot-care/. These paths are illustrative, not claims about a real website.

The product page contains a “Care and maintenance” section, but it provides no route to the guide. Our proposed change is one contextual link in that section.

Link the product care section to the boot-care guide.

The description then names the source page, the owning component, the intended destination and the reason a customer would use it: they can reach detailed care instructions while considering the product.

This is a design decision as much as a search decision. If the care section is the intended location, a match in the footer should not pass the ticket.

For the example, the expected output is ordinary link markup:

MDN documents the anchor element as a hyperlink when it has an href. A focused anchor with an href also has native Enter-key activation. Those are useful behaviours to preserve rather than trying to recreate navigation with a generic clickable element.

There is a separate search consideration. Google's crawlable-link guidance says its crawlers generally need an anchor element with an href; script events on other elements do not provide reliable URL extraction. The same guidance allows links inserted by JavaScript when the resulting markup follows those requirements.

So the ticket should require the rendered link and its destination. It should not demand a particular framework or prohibit JavaScript without a separate, evidenced reason.

For the visible label, use wording that helps explain the destination. The W3C explanation of link purpose in context describes how link text, alone or with programmatically determined context, can make a link's purpose understandable. In this example, “Read the boot-care guide” gives the reviewer a specific label to check.

Here is the acceptance contract I would use for this hypothetical ticket:

The final condition needs its own definition. Otherwise “check nothing broke” becomes another request with no useful boundary.

Suppose the care section contains an existing “Material details” accordion. The ticket changes content inside that section, so record the accordion's label, initial state and open/close behaviour before editing. Repeat that test after release.

Now suppose the same page has size selection and an add-to-basket button in a separate product-form component. Do those controls belong in this ticket's test surface?

I would decide that from the actual change and dependency paths. If the change modifies only the care-copy field, and the implementation evidence shows the purchase component and its dependencies are unchanged and independent, the ticket can stay bounded to the care section. If the work swaps a larger template or touches shared product state, that evidence no longer supports the same exclusion.

That is the point of recording ownership: establish the possible impact before choosing the regression checks. Neither physical proximity nor a different component name is enough on its own to settle the question.

This approach sits alongside the broader idea of defining verifiable requirements before code, discussed in this article on spec-driven development published on HackerNoon. The SEO-specific addition here is to name the exact public page, rendered element, and destination that must satisfy the requirement.

For this link ticket, I would retain the original care-section view, the relevant configuration or code difference, the rendered anchor, and the public after view.

Each answers a different question. The original view establishes what was there. The difference shows what changed. The rendered anchor establishes the element and destination. The public view shows the placement a visitor actually receives.

Google's JavaScript SEO documentation describes crawling, rendering and indexing as distinct processing phases. That is a reason to state which evidence view a test used. A raw-response check and an inspection of the rendered page are observations of different states; neither should be silently substituted for the other.

For this example, the useful close-out is: the agreed anchor exists once in the care section, its destination is correct, both tested activation methods work and the mapped accordion still behaves as expected.

That statement describes the delivered change. It does not claim that Google has crawled the link, indexed the guide or improved a ranking. Those are separate outcomes requiring their own evidence.

I would finish with a short record containing the public source URL, the owning section, the observed link label and destination, the tested widths, the activation results and the preserved-control result. Record any failed or unavailable check explicitly.

A saved draft or a deployed change would remain a delivery stage until those agreed checks passed. If the anchor passed but the care accordion failed, I would keep this ticket open rather than reporting only the successful half.

The useful question at handoff is simple: could another person inspect the named page and reach the same conclusion from the recorded criteria?

A good SEO ticket makes that possible. It tells engineering what to change, tells the reviewer what to observe and leaves search-performance claims for the evidence that can actually support them.

#9769. The best apples for apple pie: Here's how to choose.: We put six varieties to the test.

Which are the best pie apples? With apple-picking season hard upon us, it's time to dust off your favorite apple pie recipe, sharpen your crust-rolling skills, and get ready to enjoy fall's favorite dessert: apple pie.

You may be tempted to make your pie from one of the six apple varieties that dominate the domestic market year-round: Red Delicious, Golden Delicious, Gala, Fuji, Granny Smith, and McIntosh.

But when fall rolls around, farmers' markets and orchard farm stands offer an abundance of apple choices.

You've probably identified your favorite eating apple. But what about the best pie apples? They're not necessarily the same. Red and Golden Delicious, for instance, are reliably crisp, sweet-eating apples. But when you bake them into a pie, they can become mushy and lose some of their sweetness. So what are the best apples for pie?

We'll put six different pie apples to the test.

The pie apples: I decide to put two of my favorites, Golden Russet and Northern Spy, up against a couple of classic pie apples: McIntosh and Cortland. I also add Granny Smith because, if there's one ubiquitous, year-round apple, Granny Smith is it. Ginger Gold — a Golden Delicious cross with Albemarle Pippin — is another variety that's often available in fall, and a worthy representative of the Delicious family.

And yes, there are plenty of other apple varieties to choose from: Fuji, Gala, Honey Crisp, and so many more. But with limited time and resources — and a pan with space for just six pies — I'm not able to test every apple out there. But if you want to choose the best pie apples among your personal favorites, you can have fun doing this same test at home.

I use a muffin tin to bake apples sweetened with a bit of sugar. To mimic apple pie (sans crust), I pile sliced apples high in the pan. Then I bake them in a preheated 425°F oven for 20 minutes, lower the oven temperature to 375°F, and continue to bake the apples until they're bubbly, about 40 minutes.

I had no idea there'd be such significant differences in both texture and flavor. For example, Russets and Macs are sweetened with the same amount of sugar, bake at the same temperature, for the same amount of time —  and offer way different results.

So, Granny Smith looks like the best combination of both taste and texture. Does it make the very best apple pie?

Not necessarily. I've baked many pies with this all-purpose apple, especially during the winter when other apples are scarce or pricey. A pie made 100% with Granny Smith apples is a mighty fine pie. But in fall, when every apple variety in the world is seemingly at your fingertips, why not take advantage of one or two (or more) of your own local favorites?

At the end of the day, choosing the best pie apples is a personal decision. My best apple pie would include a combination of these three: Cortland, for flavor; Russet, for texture; and Granny Smith, for its combination of the two.

What apples would fill your best pie? Bake your favorite varieties side by side and see what happens; the results may surprise you.

#9768. Human vs. Anthropic: 11.4 Million Accounts and the Right to Digital Property

From the "Intellectual Property Law" series

11.4 million personal digital archives potentially affected.

These numbers raise an uncomfortable question about the relationship between artificial intelligence companies and the people who use their services.

The figure of 11.4 million accounts has been cited in discussions of account restrictions. It should not be interpreted as a verified count of lost archives or established legal violations.

But the underlying problem deserves serious attention.

That is the word we choose to describe what is happening.

On one side stands Anthropic, a private company entitled to establish and enforce its own terms of service.

Anthropic's terms generally recognize users' rights to outputs generated through its services, subject to applicable conditions.

On the other side stands the individual who has spent months developing projects, writing documents, creating code, and building a personal digital archive using Claude.

And the user may discover that access to years of work has disappeared.

Who owns digital content if its creator cannot access, use, or retrieve it?

We are not arguing that every decision by Anthropic to terminate a service agreement is unlawful.

A company may have legitimate reasons to restrict access to its services.

But terminating a service agreement and preventing a person from retrieving their own digital content are two different issues.

We believe users should retain meaningful rights to possess, use, and dispose of their digital materials, even after access to an AI service has been terminated.

These are fundamental principles associated with ownership.

The precise legal rights depend on the applicable jurisdiction, the nature of the content, and the contractual relationship.

Nevertheless, we believe that account suspension should not automatically result in the loss of access to a user's digital archive.

A simple text export is not always enough.

A developer may have created dozens of interconnected projects. A researcher may have organized hundreds of conversations, documents, and working materials.

Without the original structure, reconstructing that work may become extremely difficult.

We believe users should be entitled to request an archive that preserves, wherever technically possible:

A meaningful digital export should preserve not only the content but also the structure needed to understand and use it.

Consider a developer who uses Claude to work on a software project for several months.

Even if the developer retains intellectual property rights to the code, those rights may be of limited value if important project materials are inaccessible.

Ownership of digital content and the ability to retrieve that content are not the same thing.

At Ecode, we work on a related aspect of digital ownership: helping developers register cryptographic fingerprints of their code with trusted timestamps.

Such records can help document the existence of a particular file at a particular time.

They cannot restore an inaccessible Claude archive.

But both issues are connected by a broader principle: individuals should have reliable ways to document their digital work and protect their interests in it.

11.4 million accounts reportedly blocked.

How many users still need access to their projects?

How many have been unable to obtain a complete archive?

How many may have grounds to pursue legal remedies?

As Anthropic faces growing public scrutiny and discussion of a potential IPO, we believe it is especially important to address what happens to user-created content after account suspension.

We want to hear Anthropic's position on meaningful access to personal digital archives.

Aimperia and the Ecode project are collecting reports from users whose Claude accounts have been suspended.

We are examining the circumstances of these cases and assessing the possibility of a collective legal action to protect users' rights to digital content.

No conclusion has yet been reached about the legal merits of individual complaints or whether collective proceedings can be brought.

If your Claude account was suspended and you were unable to retrieve your conversations, projects, files, or other materials, we invite you to share your experience.

https://onecoderegister.io/anthropic.html

We are particularly interested in understanding whether users received their complete archives, whether exported files preserved project structures, and whether they encountered obstacles when attempting to download their data.

Digital ownership should not become meaningless when access to a service ends.

ANY.RUN provides cybersecurity solutions that help SOC and MSSP teams investigate threats, make faster and more informed decisions, and turn threat intelligence into practical actions across detection, investigation, and response.

The company’s solutions include Interactive Sandbox for enterprise malware analysis and ANY.RUN Threat Intelligence with Threat Intelligence Lookup, Threat Intelligence Feeds, and Threat Intelligence Reports. Today, ANY.RUN is trusted by more than 16,000 organizations and 700,000 security professionals worldwide. The company is SOC 2 Type II certified, with security controls designed to protect customer data.

1. What is Related Threat Context in ANY.RUN?

Related Threat Context shows whether IOCs found during an Interactive Sandbox analysis have appeared in previous team investigations, industry-related analyses, or ANY.RUN Threat Intelligence, giving SOCs and MSSPs additional context.

Related Threat Context is available to ANY.RUN Enterprise clients. Internal SOCs can access industry, team, and ANY.RUN TI context, while MSSPs can use team and ANY.RUN TI context.

3. What types of context does it provide?

Related Threat Context provides three types of context: Industry Context, Team Context, and ANY.RUN Threat Intelligence. Together, they show whether an IOC has appeared in relevant industry activity, previous team analyses, or broader TI data.

4. Does Related Threat Context determine whether an IOC is malicious?

No. Related Threat Context provides additional evidence for investigation and prioritization, but analysts still need to consider the IOC’s behavior, verdict, and other available evidence.

An industry match shows that an IOC has appeared in analyses associated with the organization’s industry. It is an additional signal, not proof that the threat is targeting that industry or a specific victim.

6. What do “Never Seen Before” and “Commonly Seen” mean?

Never Seen Before means the IOC has not previously appeared in the available related context. Commonly Seen means it has appeared frequently. Neither signal is a verdict on its own.

7. Can Related Threat Context help reduce time-to-triage?

Yes. By surfacing relevant context directly in the Sandbox, it helps analysts make faster decisions about whether to close, investigate, enrich in TI, or escalate a case.

8. Can Related Threat Context uncover additional infrastructure?

Yes. SOC and MSSP analysts can follow connections from a Sandbox IOC into Threat Intelligence Lookup to investigate related domains, samples, infrastructure, and activity that may not have been visible in the original analysis.

#9766. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9765. WordPress Critical Error Screen

Posted on Nov 3 • Originally published at kevinleary.net

Most articles on this error tell you to deactivate every plugin and switch themes until the screen goes away. That works eventually, but it is guessing. WordPress already recorded exactly what broke and where. Read that first.

“There has been a critical error on this website” is WordPress’s fatal error handler, added in 5.2. A PHP fatal error stopped the request before the page could render. Instead of a blank white page or a raw PHP error, WordPress catches it, writes it to the PHP error log, emails the site admin, and shows this generic message.

The screen itself tells you nothing about the cause. The error log does.

On a good host you can view the PHP error log from the hosting dashboard. Kinsta, WP Engine, and Cloudways all expose it; cPanel hosts usually have an “Errors” tool or an error_log file next to the site files. The error that triggered the screen will be in there, most likely at or near the top if the log is sorted newest first.

Below it you will usually see a stack trace: a numbered list of the functions that were running when the error happened, from the most recent call back to the start of the request. You rarely need to read the whole thing. The first line names the file and line that failed, and the first plugin or theme path in the trace names the code responsible.

If the host does not expose a log, turn on WordPress debug logging in wp-config.php and reload the page once:

The error is written to wp-content/debug.log. Turn WP_DEBUG back off when you are done.

When the handler catches a fatal error, WordPress emails the address set in Settings > General with the subject “Your Site is Experiencing a Technical Issue.” The email names the plugin or theme it believes is responsible and includes a link that opens the dashboard in recovery mode, where that plugin or theme is paused for your session only.

Most of the time this email is a second notice of the same thing the log already told you. It is worth opening for two reasons:

The link expires after one day by default, and WordPress rate-limits the email to one per day, so if you miss it you may not get another right away. If no email arrives, the site may not be able to send mail at all, or the error happened early enough in the request that the handler never ran. Either way, the log is still there.

Once the log or email has named the file, fix the thing that changed. In practice this error almost always follows a plugin update, a theme deploy, or a manual code edit.

Theme or custom code: if the error points at a file you or your team deployed, fix the syntax or logic error locally and redeploy. A missing semicolon, a call to a function from a plugin that is no longer active, or PHP syntax the server’s PHP version does not support are the usual suspects.

Plugin update: if the error points at a plugin that was just updated, roll it back.

Plugin conflict or PHP version: if nothing was updated, check whether the host changed the PHP version. Older plugins fail on PHP 8.x with errors like Uncaught TypeError or Call to undefined function create_function(). Rolling PHP back buys time; the real fix is replacing the plugin.

After the fix, reload the site. If it loads and you entered recovery mode, click Exit Recovery Mode in the admin bar.

Only after the above: rename wp-content/plugins to wp-content/plugins-off over SFTP. If the site loads, rename it back, then rename individual plugin folders one at a time until you find the one that breaks it. This is the method most guides lead with. It works, but it is slower than reading one line from a log.

The $30,000 average wedding figure you see everywhere is misleading. That number is skewed upward by luxury weddings in expensive metros like New York, San Francisco, and Los Angeles. The national median — the number where half of weddings cost more and half cost less — sits closer to $10,000 to $15,000. That distinction matters because it means a beautiful, memorable wedding is absolutely possible without spending five figures you do not have.

The FI perspective adds another layer: every dollar spent on a wedding is a dollar that cannot compound for decades. A $30,000 wedding invested for 30 years at a 7% average annual return grows to roughly $228,000. That does not mean you should elope in a courthouse (unless you want to), but it does mean you should spend intentionally on the categories that matter most to you and cut ruthlessly everywhere else.

Here is where the typical wedding dollar goes:

The biggest takeaway from this table: venue and catering are 60-70% of the total. If you can reduce those two categories, you change the entire math.

Not all wedding spending creates equal memories. Research consistently shows that couples remember three things most vividly years later: the ceremony itself, the food and drinks, and the photographs. Almost nobody remembers the chair covers, the napkin folds, or the custom monogram on the cocktail napkins.

That insight creates a clear FI-aligned strategy: splurge on what creates lasting memories (photographer, food, music) and minimize everything else.

The golden rule of wedding budgeting: if you cannot remember whether a detail was present at the last three weddings you attended, your guests will not notice either. Cut it without guilt.

The biggest financial mistake couples make is not setting a firm budget before visiting any vendors. Venues and vendors are skilled at upselling, and without a hard number in mind, costs spiral quickly. Start with a number you can pay in cash — wedding debt is one of the worst ways to begin a marriage and a direct threat to your FI timeline.

Follow this payment timeline to manage cash flow without credit card debt:

A practical savings strategy: divide your total budget by the number of months until the wedding and automate that transfer to a dedicated savings account. If your budget is $15,000 and your wedding is 15 months away, that is $1,000 per month. Treat it like any other savings goal on your FI path — automate, do not touch, and watch it grow.

For couples on the FI path, consider this reframe: every dollar you shave from the wedding budget is a dollar that starts compounding immediately. Cutting $5,000 from a $20,000 wedding and investing that savings at 7% for 25 years creates roughly $27,000 in future wealth. You can have a wonderful wedding and build wealth simultaneously — but only if you plan intentionally from the start.

#9763. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing

Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.
