#9713. Only One Chipotle Meat Is Cooked In-Store — And It's Not The Most Expensive Option

Chipotle is our go-to fast casual chain when we want something a little above the usual drive-thru fare, but without the fuss of a sit-down restaurant. One of the main things that sets it apart from traditional fast food is how it handles its ingredients — its stores don't even contain freezers. However, despite Chipotle's pride in its super-fresh ingredients, you might be surprised to learn that chicken is the only meat cooked from raw in its restaurants — and it isn't even the most expensive protein on the menu, clocking in at $11.95 (or $12.55 for its pollo asado) compared to $12.70 for carnitas and $13.95 for both steak and barbacoa (prices may vary).

Chipotle's top-quality chicken appears in everything from tacos and quesadillas to its iconic burritos. Unlike its other proteins, which arrive at restaurants precooked and are reheated or finished on-site, the chicken arrives raw and is later grilled in-store. Before hitting the grill, it's marinated in the chain's signature smoky adobo seasoning, helping give it that distinctive flavor. Chipotle has never publicly explained why only chicken gets this special treatment, but considering it's the chain's best-selling protein, it's hardly surprising that the company goes the extra mile to prepare it fresh.

Fortunately, you don't have to work at Chipotle to get an idea of how its chicken is prepared. Former employees have shared details of the process online, including one Redditor who explained that the chain uses boneless, skinless chicken thighs cooked on a flat-top grill coated with sunflower oil at around 475 to 500 degrees Fahrenheit until they reach a safe internal temperature of 165 degrees.

Interestingly, chicken wasn't always the only protein cooked completely from scratch in Chipotle's restaurants. Die-hard fans will remember that before 2016, the chain also prepared its steak from raw beef on-site, marinating it before cooking it on the grill. However, following a series of highly publicized and controversial food safety outbreaks in 2015, Chipotle introduced major changes to how it prepared its ingredients.

Rather than sending raw beef to its restaurants, Chipotle now uses a sous vide process, in which the steak is vacuum-sealed and cooked at a low temperature for an extended period in a controlled, off-site environment. This method allows the meat to cook evenly while helping control harmful bacteria, allegedly without sacrificing its tenderness. The steak is prepared at a central facility under USDA inspection before being shipped to restaurants, where staff season it and finish it on the grill. However, while Chipotle bosses firmly defended the new process, some customers have complained that the switch was a serious downgrade.

Chipotle's other two meat proteins, barbacoa and carnitas, have long been prepared off-site, in much the same way as each other. Barbacoa is slow-cooked beef, typically from the shoulder, while carnitas is made with pork. Both arrive at restaurants in precooked bags, where they are reheated in-store. According to one Chipotle employee on Reddit, "Carnitas comes in a pre-prepped bag, there's no actual prepping in-store or seasoning from the employees added. We take the bag, shred it up in a pot, cook it until [165 degrees Fahrenheit], then put it on the line."

#9711. For A Smokier Grilled Cheese, Make It South African-Style

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

There's truly no going wrong with a grilled cheese. With a crunchy outside and a soft, gooey interior, it's the ultimate comfort snack, even better when dunked into tomato soup – which we have actually been doing for a long time. Beyond being straight-up delicious, it's also budget-friendly, so it's no surprise there are many international variations out there. If you love grilled cheese and smoky flavors, one version you should definitely give a go is the braaibroodjie, a South African classic.

If you've never heard of a braaibroodjie, maybe don't admit that to any South Africans. The sandwich is a cultural staple, and it's a must-have side at any braai, the South African take on a barbecue. It's built from layers of cheese, sliced tomato, onion, and finished with a swipe of sweet, tangy chutney (Mrs. Ball's is the classic choice, which is available online), all tucked between buttered slices of white bread. There's plenty of room for variation without losing what makes it so delicious in the first place, and some less traditional recipes call for extra ingredients like mayo, chili, or even pineapple.

But what really sets a braaibroodjie apart from your standard skillet grilled cheese is how it's cooked. The clue is in the name; the Afrikaans word braai comes from the Dutch word braden (meaning to roast or grill), while broodjie is the diminutive of brood (Dutch for bread). Combined, it roughly translates to "little barbecue bread." In typical barbecue style, instead of a pan, the sandwich is clamped into a hinged grill basket and toasted slowly over glowing coals. That low, steady heat gently toasts the bread and melts the cheese, while the rising smoke from the coals infuses the sandwich with a subtle smokiness a frying pan simply doesn't have the facilities to deliver.

A braaibroodjie is already a pretty perfect sandwich, but that doesn't mean you can't have a little fun with the formula. For a more filling, high-protein braaibroodjie, add shredded chicken, thin slices of steak, or even some canned tuna. If you prefer a deeper balance of sweet and smoky flavors, swap raw onions for slowly caramelized ones to bring out their natural sweetness and add a richer, more savory depth to the sandwich.

The ingredients are the easy part, and the biggest obstacle most home cooks will face when making a braaibroodjie is the cooking itself. The beauty of a grilled cheese is its simplicity, and that doesn't just apply to the ingredients. For many, tending a bed of glowing coals defeats the entire purpose of a low-effort sandwich, and for plenty of us, it isn't even feasible, especially if you're cooking in an apartment with no backyard in sight. If you want to capture the smoky essence of a braaibroodjie without breaking out the matches and charcoal, there are other ways to go about it.

If you want a smoky braaibroodjie that's safe to make indoors, try tweaking your ingredients rather than your cooking method. The easiest place to start is with ingredients that already make up the foundation of the sandwich. Instead of plain old cheddar, swap in smoked cheddar. For an extra-stretchy cheese pull, reach for smoked mozzarella, or smoked scamorza (an Italian stretched-curd cheese, similar to mozzarella but firmer) for an even richer flavor. If you're feeling a little more adventurous, stir some bacon jam into your chutney, or even add a drop or two of liquid smoke — but remember, it's potent, so a little goes a long way.

#9708. Add This Italian-Style Topping To Your Salami Sandwich For A Taste Of New Orleans

If you ever want to expand on a basic salami sandwich, it's never a bad choice to first look to New Orleans, a city famous for its vibrant culinary history. However, the best topping isn't necessarily a roux-rich sauce or some fried shrimp, but olive salad, a rich, tangy, vegetable-forward topping that works perfectly with cured salami.

When people think of New Orleans-style cuisine, they often think first of Cajun and Creole spice mixes, French techniques, and classic staples like the po'boy. But the city has never had a shortage of Italian heritage, which eventually gave rise to olive salad, a vital component of its famous muffuletta. While salami is a common ingredient in this sandwich, a dollop of olive salad alone won't make it one. Still, the unique blend of oil, acid, and salt pairs perfectly with the cured fattiness of salami, delivering an almost creamy texture as you bite through the minced drupes.

While it may seem redundant to pair a tangy meat with a tangy condiment, it's much like adding horseradish to a capsaicin-rich cocktail sauce to create two different types of heat. The ingredients work together to deliver multiple nuances of the same type of flavor, making the taste complex but still quite focused. Pair it with some nice bread to soak up the oil, and you've got a dynamite, three-ingredient meal that tastes like it was made by a true expert.

Creating a truly New Orleans-style olive salad takes a bit of time. While some coarsely chopped canned black olives can add flavor to a salami sandwich, picking the right blend, breaking them down just right, and letting them marinate imparts a greater depth of flavor that makes this topping truly special.

For a more comprehensive range of flavors, use a mix of black and green olives. Kalamatas are always a solid choice thanks to the strength of their flavor, but the large black ones at a salad bar work just fine as well. For your greens, Giada De Laurentiis prefers Castelvetranos, a rich, buttery-soft variety that has next to no bitterness. It's also quite common to add all sorts of pickled vegetables, from carrots and garlic to cauliflower and giardiniera blends, so just about anything veggie- and acid-based will do.

A good olive salad doesn't have the paste-like consistency of tapenade, but it should be soft and tender enough to chew through easily. It's best to chop the ingredients by hand, but you can still use a food processor so long as you stick to quick pulses and avoid smushing everything too much. Letting everything marinate together is vital to bringing out the best in this recipe, so let things sit in your fridge for at least a day. Olive salad can last for weeks in the fridge when properly prepared and stored, so feel free to make a big batch and enjoy it over time.

#9707. Does β‑Blocker Use Increase Depression Risk?

The association between β-blocker use and depression was investigated in a population-based observational study recently published in the journal Drug Safety.

While depression is often cited as an adverse effect of β-blocker use, there is limited evidence supporting this causal relationship. To better understand the association between beta blockers and the risk of new-onset depression, the study authors analyzed data from the UK population-based Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) GOLD database.

“We identifed patients aged 18-80 years with an incident depression diagnosis between 2000 and 2016, and matched controls, and estimated the risk (odds ratio [OR]) of depression in association with use of β-blockers,” the study authors explained.

Findings of the analysis revealed an increased risk of developing depression among short-term users of β-blockers compared with no use at all (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.91; 95% CI, 1.72-2.12).

Among short-term users, increased risk of depression was mainly restricted to patients with a neuropsychiatric disorder taking propranolol (aOR 6.33, 95% CI 5.16–7.76).  Patients on propranolol for a cardiovascular indication were found to be at slightly elevated risk of depression (aOR 1.44, 95% CI 1.14–1.82). Apart from propranolol, no other lipophilic β-blocker or hydrophilic β-blocker was found to increase the risk of depression.

Additionally, no association was observed between long-term use of β-blockers and the risk of depression (aOR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.85-0.94).

“Our findings suggest that the reported association between use of β-blockers and depression may not be causal but rather a result of protopathic bias,” the study authors concluded.

Bornand D, Reinau D, Jick SS, Meier CR. β‑blockers and the risk of depression: A matched case–control study. Drug Safety. Published online January 19, 2022. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40264-021-01140-5.

#9702. 5 Breakfast Sausage Brands That Use High-Quality Ingredients (And 2 To Avoid)

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Breakfast sausage is a great addition to your breakfast by itself, on a biscuit as part of a sausage, egg, and cheese biscuit, or as part of a scramble. But to make sure you're getting the best quality out there, we've created a list of sausage brands that use high-quality ingredients, as well as those you'd probably want to avoid. We looked at how the animals are treated, if they're given growth hormones or excessive antibiotics, and whether the resulting sausage is minimally processed. We also made sure there were no artificial ingredients or excessive fillers.

It might seem like a small thing to look for products with high quality ingredients, but the benefits are many. Chief among them is the positive difference in taste. Breakfast and dinner sausages already taste different, thanks to the addition of sage in the breakfast versions. But high-quality ingredients and meat also taste more savory and often keep you feeling fuller for longer because of the lack of fillers. That can keep the protein high, making the quality sausage a good choice for those watching their macros. So, if you want the best value for your money, alongside the best tasting breakfast sausages, keep this list handy the next time you visit the grocery store.

Applegate Organics has been in business for nearly 40 years, and in that time, the brand has earned a strong reputation as one of the meat industry's most trustworthy companies, thanks to its transparency with customers. The brand's various breakfast sausages are often cited by chefs as a high-quality product because the company takes animal welfare seriously and doesn't use antibiotics on any of the animals it sources.

The pigs used for pork sausage aren't kept in crates, which allows them to be less stressed and gain natural muscle from wandering. They're fed an all vegetarian diet, so there's no animal byproducts in the feed. Applegate's poultry, like turkeys and chickens, are also fed all plant-based diets and given more room to move. This keeps the air quality in the facilities better, which leads to fewer health problems for the animals.

The poultry even get environmental enrichments that allow them to keep their natural perching, scratching, and pecking behaviors, which keeps their stress down and leads to better tasting meat. All of the resulting sausages from the pigs and birds are made without nitrates, preservatives, or artificial ingredients.

Pederson's Natural Farms has been in the pork business since 1992. It only sold three types of bacon when it opened, but the business has greatly expanded since then. The brand now includes beef and bison in addition to a multitude of pork products. All of the meats come from animals that have been raised humanely through sustainable practices, and many of them are certified organic.

This company uses heritage Duroc swine for its breakfast sausages and other pork products. The swine are allowed to roam and fed a vegetarian diet. It has a no antibiotics policy and doesn't use steroids or other growth hormones on the pigs, and the resulting sausages are made without nitrates or nitrites as preservatives. If you're wondering why that matters (because you'll see them mentioned a lot on this list), nitrates and nitrites in processed meats have been linked with high blood pressure and other cardiovascular diseases.

The company doesn't add sugar to them during processing, making the sausages Whole30 Approved, as well as acceptable for those maintaining a keto or paleo lifestyle. The breakfast meat is made with simple ingredients, but no artificial ones are allowed. Pederson's sausages are also certified gluten free, as well as animal welfare certified.

Bob Evans is one of the most recognized names in dinner sides and meat products in supermarkets today. But not everyone is happy with the products Bob Evan's makes, primarily because of a lack of transparency around its practices and potentially problematic preservatives.

The mass-produced brand has no information about animal welfare on its website, unlike the Bob Evans Farmhouse Kitchen, which advertises a commitment to animal welfare and general sustainability. What is known about the breakfast sausages is that preservatives like potassium lactate, BHA, and BHT are used to keep the meat from spoiling. Potassium lactate acts as a way to enhance flavor, hold moisture and keep the product fresh longer, and is generally considered safe to consume.

However, BHA and BHT are a different story. BHA has been under investigation by the European Union since 2018 as a potential endocrine disruptor, which can have concerning effects on animal and human reproductive health. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration began its own inquiry into the preservative in early 2026. BHT is suspected to cause damage to the lungs, kidneys, and liver after repeated exposure, but no formal studies by the FDA are currently underway. Coupled with multiple complaints about animal welfare, Bob Evans is a brand you might want to avoid.

Primal Pastures bills itself as the cleanest meat in America. Started in 2012, this company uses domestically raised and slaughtered pigs that are made into sausage with no fillers. All of its swine are grass fed, with no soy or corn to supplement their feed, and pasture raised, which allows them to be less stressed and attain muscle naturally. All of the brand's meats are also certified humane in Southern California where its processing facility is located.

The pork used in Primal Pasture's breakfast sausages is raised in Nebraska, where they're allowed to roam freely and graze. The farmers rotate the swine from pasture to pasture, ensuring there's always new grass for them to eat. The pigs are never given vaccines or antibiotics, and the sausages are made with no preservatives or artificial ingredients. In fact, the ground pork sausage is made with only six ingredients, while the links are made with seven, including pork, black pepper, sea salt, allspice, sage, celery seed, and a collagen casing.

Jones Dairy Farm might seem like an odd name for a company that primarily sells pork products, but the brand has been selling sausages since the late 1800s. So even though the farm was originally for dairy cows, its claim to fame became high quality pork made from a family recipe. More than a century later, the company is still committed to the welfare of its animals and to using simple ingredients in its products, such as its large variety of breakfast sausages.

This brand makes the breakfast meats in pork, chicken, and turkey. None of the sausages have MSG, fillers, or nitrates included. There's a line of the meats that have no antibiotics ever used on the animals, and none of the sausages contain gluten. The All Natural Pork Sausage Roll has even qualified for the Master Chefs' Institute's Seal of Excellence, thanks in part to its excellent flavor. Jones Dairy Farm breakfast sausages have also earned a spot as one of the items Food Republic taste-testers will always repurchase.

If you frequent the freezer aisles in nearly any grocery store, you'll be familiar with the yellow and red packaging Banquet uses for its Brown 'N Serve breakfast sausages. This budget brand has been around since the 1950s and makes everything from pot pies to frozen dinners to family meals. But it might be most famous for its large selection of breakfast sausages. Unfortunately, many people know the meat for its poor quality, with some calling the brand the worst sausages in the freezer aisle. The brand even took last place on Food Republic's ranking of popular breakfast sausage brands in 2025.

Along with using lower-quality meats, the brand uses BHA and BHT as preservatives. The sausages have a high percentage of soy protein concentrate added as a filler to give the meat more volume and inflate the amount of protein. The meat is also ultra-processed. All in all, this is one to avoid, despite the brand's nostalgic allure.

Niman Ranch might've started as a cattle-based operation in the 1970s, but as soon as the company began partnering with hog farmers in the mid-1990s, the brand never looked back. The company now has a network of over 600 farms and ranches working to raise the best cattle, sheep, and swine in the country. Every animal that Niman Ranch uses for its meat products never has antibiotics or added hormones given to them, and each supplier has to meet strict guidelines for the treatment of the animals and sustainability practices. All of that hard work shows in the taste and quality of the breakfast sausages the company sells.

The breakfast meats are gluten-free and come from pigs that are Certified Humane by the Humane Farm Animal Care program. The swine are fed a 100% vegetarian diet with no animal byproducts, which greatly reduces the chances of the pigs getting sick. The resulting sausage is minimally processed and uncured, so there are no added nitrates or nitrites. You could even try this breakfast meat in this upgraded take on pigs in a blanket.

To find the best and worst breakfast sausages, we combed through the numerous brands that make the product before honing in on how the companies raised and treated the animals. If they were given growth hormones, excessive antibiotics, or low-quality feed, they went on the avoid list. If the animals were treated well and the resulting sausage was minimally processed with no fillers or artificial ingredients, it went on the buy list.

We then narrowed down the buy and avoid lists by looking specifically at customer's reactions to the product's taste and overall value on social media, user review sites, message boards, and professional reviews. The resulting list has what we believe are the best and worst breakfast sausages determined by multiple quality indicators and customer satisfaction.

#9700. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.

High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.

The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.

To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.

High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.

High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.

You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.

Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.

If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.

Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.

Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.

Find our high-extraction Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour online.

#9698. What's The Difference Between Yellow And White Chicken Skin?

Between mass-producing farms and local businesses, chicken comes in no small amount of variety. When most people first encounter yellow chicken skin, they can be shocked at the color difference and possibly even think the meat has spoiled. However, this isn't an indication of freshness, but rather the life the chicken had before processing.

Differences in skin color come from a number of factors, and genetics can play a major role. Some lineages are more prone to developing white, yellow, or even black skin. Still, more often than not, the color of chicken skin is due to something called carotenoids, a type of pigment that finds its way into chicken fat. Chickens raised on a processed diet may not get as much of this in their feed, so their skin ends up the familiar, pearly white. Poultry fed through grazing or given kitchen scraps or even corn can pick up enough of this pigment that it tends to dye their fat, much of which is found beneath their skin.

Just like how grass-fed beef tastes different, a chicken with yellow fat can taste quite distinct. If left to graze most of its life, it may taste a bit more complex, with a slight gaminess. In some cases, corn-fed breeds may also develop more fat, making them taste richer. Still, freshness, point of origin, and size are the important factors when selecting the most flavorful chicken at the store.

Whether you're roasting a whole bird or looking to make some crackling, white skin on a chicken is a familiar choice for most people. When prepared properly, it can develop a uniform, golden-brown hue with great flavor and has enough fat and collagen to make a perfectly good stock.

If you're feeding a crowd, it's often best to go with consistency and familiarity to appeal to a broader range of palates. While you may prefer a bit of nuance in your poultry, a white-skinned chicken is often a safe choice. While it may not have quite the complexity of a free-range, grazing bird, it can still have just as much flavor. While not a 100% exact correlation, white-skinned broiler chickens raised in conventional farming operations also tend to be larger than free-range, grazing ones raised at a slower pace on farms equipped to let them have a more varied diet.

While corn can contribute to fat development in everything from cows to chickens, it doesn't necessarily make for the richest poultry available. A plump chicken with white skin may still have had a fairly varied diet, as skin color isn't a reliable indicator of what it ate. Ultimately, the best way to determine a chicken's fat content is to break it down and look for yourself.

From lambs to chickens to humans, beta-carotene is a pigment that can accumulate in fat deposits. More marbled cuts, like dark meat, carry a greater amount of fat and a subtly rich flavor, making them invaluable in certain recipes. If you use skin or fat as a specialty ingredient, yellow-skinned birds can be a great way to add intense meatiness.

Just like lard or tallow, chicken fat is an incredibly potent cooking fat with a respectably high smoke point once clarified. In particular, Jewish communities have a long history of making schmaltz, rendered chicken fat often made from skin and sometimes seasoned with aromatics. Whether you're keeping it on hand in the fridge or adding chicken drippings to Alfredo sauce, it's important to use only a small amount to prevent things from becoming greasy. In this case, you want the most flavorful ingredient possible, and that can start with a yellow-skinned bird raised on a varied diet.

When made right, chicken skin crackling can be better than bacon. While you can always add seasonings to upgrade it, those looking to focus more on the "chicken flavor" of the ingredient may see better results with yellow-skinned birds. Both white- and yellow-skin cracklings are undeniably tasty, but ones made from yellow skin may need only a little sprinkle of salt and a trip to the oven to be truly marvelous. Even if you don't plan on using it right away, any leftover skin from a yellow chicken is always worth saving.

#9696. Forget Pricey Prime Rib: The Cheaper Cut With Rich, Beefy Flavor

Prime rib is among the most coveted beef cuts. Hailing from the same well-marbled region as ribeye steak, it's a section of meat that's both ultra-flavorful and tender. Typically roasted in a large, multipound intact piece, it's a delicious cut of beef that's slow-cooked, all while retaining a medium-rare interior. Undoubtedly, it's a tasty experience — however, a quality prime rib can cost upward of $20 a pound. Considering 10 pounds is a standard size, the bill adds up quickly.

Thankfully, though, there is a cheaper alternative to consider: a chuck roast. This huge, beefy cut comes from a region directly adjacent to the prime rib, roughly around the animal's shoulder area. In composition, chuck roast offers many similarities to prime rib. While not quite of the same decadent fat density, the cut also contains abundant marbling, as well as a strong beefy flavor. Yet the cost is drastically lower, with chuck roast often available for between $7 and $10 a pound. At around 2 to 4 pounds, it's much more reasonable.

Most often, chuck roast is slow-cooked until well-done, as seen in dishes like beef bourguignon, a favorite of Julia Child's. Yet don't sleep on preparing larger versions of the cut to medium-rare, just like prime rib. Pair a carefully selected chuck cut with the right technique, and the dish offers a similar culinary experience at a fraction of the price.

Not every chuck roast works for a prime rib-like preparation. You'll want to grab a cut with less connective tissue than other parts of the chuck, where it's common. Look specifically for a chuck eye roast, a type of chuck roast that sits right next to the ribeye and thus offers more marbling. In order to recreate the meaty prime rib experience, opt for a larger chuck eye roast — typically around 2 to 3 pounds (larger 5-pound cuts may include tougher surrounding muscles). Especially when topped with a fat cap, such a purchase can help keep the beef moist and flavorful as it cooks.

From here on out, you can cook the chuck eye roast using prime rib-style seasonings, but use a low-temperature cooking method rather than a standard high-heat roast to promote even cooking. You'll want to tie up the beef with twine to promote a uniform shape, as well as add seasonings of choice. Chuck eye roast shines with varied preparation methods, whether a low-temperature reverse sear (low oven or smoker followed by a quick pan-sear) or a temperature-controlled sous vide bath. Cook to medium-rare, rest uncovered for several minutes, then slice. You'll get a mouthwatering prime rib experience at a fraction of the price.

#9692. Scrambled Eggs Won't Be Same When You Grab A Canned Staple With Extra Protein

For a lot of people, scrambled eggs are a go-to when it comes time for a hot, savory breakfast. And why not? They're quick and easy to make, and they've long been considered the gold standard for protein, coming in at roughly 6 to 7 grams apiece.

All that said, though, on their own, scrambled eggs are more of a side, but if you want to make them main meal-worthy, adding one staple ingredient will not only bring more flavor into the mix, but a great deal of extra protein, too. Canned tuna is the game-changer here — it infuses your eggs with a savory umami flavor reminiscent of the sea, as well as a satisfyingly meaty texture.

You could partially scramble your eggs, then add the tuna and continue to cook until the eggs are set, or even mix the tuna and raw, cracked eggs in a bowl and pour both into the pan together. But we highly recommend working in steps, first draining the liquid from the can (don't rinse the fish!) and crisping up the tuna in a hot skillet with some oil, then adding the eggs and cooking until they're set. This gives the tuna a delightful texture boost, and it makes for a much more interesting bite with the contrasting crispy bits of the fish and the softness of the eggs.

Tuna and scrambled eggs are endlessly modifiable, which is great if you take comfort in making the same dishes on repeat, but need a little flavor variation. You might try first switching up the tuna you're using; StarKist's Flavor Fresh Pouch line, for example, has a wide selection of flavors, everything from Honey BBQ to Jalapeño to Thai Chili. Even better, you don't have to drain anything — you can just dump the tuna straight from the pouch into the skillet.

If you're looking to build a little flavor in the oil before you add the tuna, though, you might chop or mince some fresh onion or garlic, respectively. Red onion in particular is an excellent aromatic to use because it imbues the whole dish with a kiss of sweetness that contrasts deliciously with the savory elements. Or you might really lean into the fish factor with a splash of fish sauce and a liquid sweetener, like honey or maple syrup, both to develop deep, savory notes and to allow the sugars to promote super-flavorful caramelization of the tuna.

And then there are toppings. A sprinkle of green onion would add an appealing brightness and bite to this dish, while those looking for outright spice might finish off the tuna and scrambled eggs with a drizzle of hot sauce or sriracha. Or you could shovel the tuna-and-egg combination onto sturdy pieces of toast and top with avocado and plenty of everything bagel seasoning.

#9688. Pour Cream Over Diced Potatoes For A Southern-Style Side (Hint: It's Not Gratin)

Cream and potatoes go together better than peanut butter and jelly, and with only a few extra fixings, you can get a seriously Southern-style side dish with very little effort. By just combining potatoes, seasoning, and cream, you get Creole potatoes, a rustic, flavorful recipe with tons of room for experimentation. Enter: Creole cream potatoes.

When it comes to Creole cooking, you'll often find some sort of vegetable gratin on the menu. However, whereas a standard gratin relies on a roux to thicken a cream sauce, this recipe keeps the sauce a bit thinner. Using Creole spice mix instead of Cajun is also quite important, as the higher ratio of herbs pairs perfectly with a bit of cheese, dairy fat, and tubers. While you still want a bit of spice, the parsley, oregano, thyme, and other woody herbs diffuse their flavorful oils into the sauce to then be absorbed by the potatoes.

Since you won't be able to taste this dish as you go, you may want to use a different kind of butter than your usual salted variety. Unsalted ones give you maximum control and, while potatoes do absorb sodium quite well, this is important so that you don't spend an hour baking a dish you later find unpalatable. Most of the baking time for this recipe calls for it to be covered, but don't forget a final few minutes uncovered or even under the broiler to crisp up a last layer of cheese and roast any exposed parts of the potatoes. A little crunch in a swimming rich sauce of cream? Yes, please.

When you're working with such a simple dish, there's always room to add new ingredients or try out new preparation methods. Whether you're picking out different potatoes for a new texture, finding the right balance of fat, or even tossing in some protein, it's hard to go wrong with something this straightforward.

If you like your sauce to be a bit thicker, something that clings to the vegetables, try using russet potatoes. Affordable and available most anywhere, these come loaded with starch but have very little moisture, making them perfect for baking with dairy. This same thing makes them the best variety of spud for scalloped potatoes as they're great at absorbing fat and keeping that flavor on your fork rather than pooling at the bottom of the dish. If you want to keep your sauce thin, aim for a waxier potato, like fingerlings, new potatoes, or any red variety.

Speaking of fat, the one downside of any cream- and butter-based recipe is that it's easy to make it overly greasy. Full-fat cream is vital to getting the right mouthfeel and flavor for the sauce, but you can always use a lower-fat butter or leaner protein as your main. Leaving fat out of other ingredients can also be an opportunity for adding it back through other means. Few things are more Creole than classic potatoes and sausage, but if you want to have less oil, there's no protein more lean and Louisiana than shrimp.

#9686. What are flour enzymes?: Understanding a common flour ingredient.

If you look closely at a bag of King Arthur flour, you may see an unfamiliar ingredient listed there: enzyme.

We’re extremely thoughtful about every ingredient we use, across all King Arthur products and recipes. Our Food Philosophy guides every decision to ensure the quality of what we create, and that includes the enzymes in our flour.

Here’s exactly what flour enzymes are and why they’re included in flour.

Enzymes are found naturally in wheat, and thus are already present in flour. An enzyme is a protein produced by a living organism that acts as a catalyst to bring about a specific biochemical reaction.

The amount of enzymes in flour can vary based on growing conditions from harvest to harvest and year to year, so we add natural enzymes to correct for any variance and make sure our flour bakes more consistently — in other words, to make your baking even better. Those enzymes make up a very small portion of the total flour: less than 1%.

The enzyme we use in our flour is technically called fungal alpha-amylase. That’s a pretty technical name, so it is commonly labeled simply as “enzyme” on ingredient labels. “Alpha-amylase” is the actual enzyme, and “fungal” refers to the fact that the living organism that produces the enzyme is a fungus, not unlike yeast or a mushroom. Amylase may sound unfamiliar, but your body makes and uses it every day. When you eat, it begins breaking starch into smaller carbohydrates so you can draw on it for energy. Amylases added to flour perform a similar function.

Note: Though fungi are technically living organisms, enzymes are considered vegan, as they are not animal based.

Malted barley is an alternative source of enzymes that King Arthur has used in the past, but we found the efficacy can vary batch to batch. By swapping malted barley for straight enzymes, the flour produces more consistent results for our bakers.

Another reason we made the switch? Enzymes require less water and energy to produce than malt barley. As a Certified B Corporation, we're committed to being good stewards of our planet, so pivoting to a responsibly sourced ingredient with a smaller environmental footprint makes sense.

To put it simply, enzymes are added to flours to improve baking performance — they do not change the flour's nutritional value. More specifically, they help create the foods that feeds yeasts. The enzymes break down complex starches into simpler sugars; this, in turn, provides yeast with readily available fermentable sugar (food!), which enables yeast to work continuously and supports both fermentation and crust browning. This results in improved bread volume and crumb texture. Most other manufacturers of flour and yeasted mixes use enzymes for the very same reasons.

Ultimately, enzymes are yet another way for us to provide you with the most consistent flour — which means even better baking.

Cover photo and food styling by Liz Neily.

#9684. James Bond Ate This Vintage Breakfast You Rarely See On Menus Anymore

Whether it's the Rolex watches or a seemingly endless supply of Aston Martins, few encapsulate luxury quite like James Bond. The iconic spy from Ian Fleming's novels has long been a cultural icon, and his taste for the finer things extends well beyond material possessions. When it comes to dining, everyone knows his "shaken, not stirred" martini order, along with his fondness for Bollinger Champagne, scrambled eggs, and Beluga caviar. But only eagle-eyed fans who have read Fleming's 1958 novel "Dr No" may recall 007 tucking into grilled kidneys, an old-school delicacy that's seriously underrated by modern diners.

In the novel, Bond is held captive by the titular villain, but his captors don't exactly skimp on the prison food. His morning meal consisted of scrambled eggs on toast, four rashers of bacon, an English pork sausage, and a grilled kidney, alongside rolls, preserves, pineapple juice, and coffee with cream. It's a surprisingly lavish spread for a prisoner, although the kidney may raise a few eyebrows among younger readers. Back in the day, however, offal was a favorite amongst boomers, and kidneys were a welcome addition to a hearty breakfast.

Kidneys were a part of a long tradition of morning meals, particularly among the well-to-do during the Victorian and Edwardian eras, so it was almost inevitable that they'd later feature in a Bond novel. Back in the early 20th century, you could expect to find this dish served at all manner of haughty establishments, like the Fairmont San Francisco, and they're still served for breakfast at London's ultra-fancy Dorchester Hotel. Fleming leaves how they're prepared to the imagination, but one common recipe involves halving the kidneys lengthways, removing the tough inner core, and grilling both sides for no more than three minutes, brushing them with butter throughout.

Beyond looking as suave as Bond, there are plenty of reasons to give kidneys a spot on your shopping list. Aside from being relatively inexpensive, they're nutritional powerhouses, packed with protein and essential nutrients. It's also worth considering from a sustainability standpoint. Organ meats make up a substantial portion of a livestock carcass, yet they're often overlooked in favor of more familiar cuts. In fact, a 2019 study for Environmental Science & Technology examining Germany's meat industry found that increasing offal consumption by 50% could reduce the sector's greenhouse gas emissions by up to 14%, partly because adopting a nose-to-tail philosophy means fewer animals would be needed to meet demand.

One of the biggest hurdles to cooking kidneys is simply knowing where to start. They aren't your everyday chicken breast or steak, so preparing them for the first time can feel daunting. But here's the secret: They're not nearly as tricky as you might think. Pan-frying is a classic method, particularly for making deviled kidneys. Slice the kidneys in half and cut out the tough white core. Fry them in butter until browned, then add a punchy mixture of your favorite jelly, mustard, Worcestershire sauce, and a pinch of cayenne pepper. Let everything bubble together briefly, thicken the sauce with cream, and then spoon it all over buttered toast for a super traditional British breakfast.

Sometimes half the battle is getting past the idea of what you're eating. To counter this, you can even sneak kidneys into everyday meals without making them the star of the show. Ask your butcher to mince them, then mix a small amount into ground lamb or beef for a rich, savory ragù, shepherd's pie, or even homemade burger patties. If you're feeling really adventurous, skip the mince and combine the kidneys with chopped livers and heart.

#9682. The Elephant in the Rheum – “Burnout” Among the Workforce

Feelings of stress, fatigue, and exhaustion – what is being described as “burnout” – have become a common occurrence among providers, including rheumatologists, with important implications in clinical practice. Various surveys and studies have reported a substantial prevalence of burnout (approximately 50%) among rheumatology providers.

Beth L. Jonas, MD, Reeves Foundation Distinguished Professor of Medicine and chief of the Division of Rheumatology, Allergy, and Immunology at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (UNC), joins us on this episode to provide deeper insight on the issue of “burnout” from a clinical practice standpoint.

Read the full transcript of the episode here.

Beth L. Jonas, MD, is the Reeves Foundation Distinguished Professor of Medicine and chief of the Division of Rheumatology, Allergy, and Immunology at UNC.

A recipient of a 2015 Rheumatology Research Foundation (RRF) Clinician Scholar Educator Award, Dr Jonas has developed a novel curriculum in Rheumatology in the Foundation Phase at UNC. She is a clinician educator and has an active rheumatology practice, where she sees patients with a wide spectrum of inflammatory rheumatic disorders. She teaches rheumatology to medical students, residents, and fellows and is actively involved in curricular development to train both physicians and advance practice providers in rheumatology.

Dr Jonas currently serves on the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) Workforce Solutions Committee. She has previously served as the chair of the ACR Committee on Training and Workforce and has served as co-chair of the ACR In-Training Examination Taskforce. She has served on the board of the Rheumatology Research Foundation as well as the RRF Scientific Advisory Committee.

Dr Jonas is a founding member of the Carolinas Fellows Collaborative (CFC), a group of program directors from the Carolinas who work to enhance the education of their collective trainees. Dr Jonas was honored as the ACR Distinguished Rheumatology Program Director in 2015.

This article originally appeared on Rheumatology Advisor

Psychiatry Advisor, a trusted source of medical news and feature content for healthcare providers, offers clinicians insight into the latest research to inform clinical practice and improve patient outcomes.

#9679. The Companies Allegedly Behind 15 Trader Joe's Items

Trader Joe's is full of unique and delicious products sold under the brand's private label, but having the store's name on the package doesn't mean that's who is making those products. Like other private label retailers like Aldi and Costco, Trader Joe's keeps the identity of its vendors under wraps to help keep costs lower for consumers. This probably means very little to the average Trader Joe's customer until beloved Trader Joe's products are discontinued and the search for a suitable replacement begins.

Importantly, just because a brand is confirmed or believed to be behind a Trader Joe's product doesn't mean that the Trader Joe's item is identical to the brand's usual offering. Small recipe or ingredient changes to adhere to Trader Joe's product standards and vendor requirements aren't uncommon.

Still, knowing the vendor can help you find a close match. While the legal agreements that keep Trader Joe's brands a secret usually make it nearly impossible to confirm the companies behind the store's products, several brands have been outed over the years. This is thanks to a combination of discerning customers, loose lipped employees, and a food safety policy that errs on the side of caution, resulting in an abundance of Trader Joe's recalls.

When it comes to foods like nuts, it's nearly impossible to tell one brand from another simply by looking at them, especially if the nuts in question don't have any special seasonings or flavors. That's certainly the case for pistachios roasted in their shells, which look virtually identical across brands, but a 2016 Salmonella-related recall helped unmask the major brand behind Trader Joe's pistachios as Wonderful Pistachios.

Three versions of Trader Joe's dry roasted, in shell pistachios were included in the recall: salted, unsalted, and 50% less salt. While the shelled version of Trader Joe's pistachios (unroasted, unsalted pistachio nutmeats) were not included in the recall and therefore can't definitively be linked to Wonderful, it is notable that the packaging for the shelled version is nearly identical to the dry roasted, in shell version, and Trader Joe's notes that both versions originate in California. Take that for what it's worth.

Salad kits and prepared salads are a convenient way to add extra veggies to your meal, and Trader Joe's has some delicious options. The brand behind those salads is one you've almost certainly heard. In August 2026, a large recall for fresh jalapeños contaminated with Salmonella had ripple effects across the food industry because of the number of brands that used the peppers in its products. Among those was Taylor Farms, which issued a recall on a number of different products, including Trader Joe's fiesta style salad with shrimp sold in Texas.

Around the same time, during a large scale outbreak of Cyclospora related illnesses also linked to Taylor Farms, an alleged Trader Joe's employee revealed on Reddit that the store sources most of its salad kits from Taylor Farms. At the time, the source of those illnesses had not yet been narrowed down to iceberg lettuce, and the seemingly well meaning employee posted the revelation as a public service announcement. The outbreak was declared over by the Centers for Disease Control on September 11, 2026.

Many Trader Joe's prepared foods and meals are perfect for a picnic, and you might be surprised how many of them are made by the same company. Bakkavor Foods USA has been behind many Trader Joe's products for at least a decade and was one of the largest producers of fresh and prepared foods in both the United States and the UK before being acquired by Greencore in 2025.

In 2016, Bakkavor issued a voluntary recall of both Trader Joe's Mediterranean Hummus and White Bean & Basil Hummus due to possible contamination with Listeria monocytogenes. But hummus isn't the only food that Bakkavor produces for Trader Joe's. Three years later in 2019, another voluntary recall was issued, again for possible listeria contamination, but this time in Trader Joe's Egg Salad and Old Fashioned Potato Salad. Then, in 2023, the company issued a recall for Trader Joe's Genova Pesto because it was incorrectly packaged and contained undeclared allergens in the form of milk and walnuts, both of which can cause serious allergic reactions.

After being acquired by Greencore, Bakkavor issued another recall in 2026 for Trader Joe's Focaccia Bread with Roasted Tomato & Parmesan. Metal fragments were discovered in the bread, which the company later said came from its roasted tomato supplier.

While the sugar content and some of the health claims made by Naked Juice have come under fire over the years, there's no denying that the brand makes delicious juice and smoothies. To hear some customers tell it, those same juices can be found at Trader Joe's.

Based on labels alone, those customers may be onto something. The ingredients in Trader Joe's Very Green 100% juice smoothie are a very close match to Naked's Green Machine and Trader Joe's Mango 100% juice smoothie is virtually a carbon copy of Naked's Mighty Mango Machine.

While that may be as close as we can get to confirmation today, Naked Juice and Trader Joe's go back more than two decades. In 2000, when possible Salmonella contamination resulted in a fresh juice recall in California, both Naked Juice and Trader Joe's juice were included as both were sourced from California Day-Fresh Foods at the time.

Naked Juice isn't the only brand behind the juice at Trader Joe's, at least as of 2024. Back then, a recall of under-processed organic carrot juice that carried a risk of causing botulism revealed that Trader Joe's organic carrot juice was made by Barsotti. It really wasn't that much of a surprise given that the Barsotti bottle was virtually identical to the Trader Joe's bottle, from the shape all the way down (or up) to the green cap.

Still, it was good for the carrot juice lovers to get confirmation, especially because Trader Joe's does not currently sell the organic carrot juice, and many customers miss it. Based on social media posts, it seemed to disappear from Trader Joe's shelves right around the time of the recall and never reappeared.

Trader Joe's does list an organic carrot turmeric juice blend on its website, but Barsotti does not sell a similar juice blend. Still, it's possible the carrot juice in the current juice blend originates with Barsotti and is a special recipe exclusive for Trader Joe's, but at this point, that's merely speculation.

While it is just one of many Trader Joe's myths that've been debunked that the grocery store is a spot for health food, the company does have pretty stringent standards for its products, and organic foods are easy to find. Combining both organic ingredients and a popular comfort food, the organic shells and white cheddar macaroni and cheese is long believed to be the same as Annie's organic Shells & White Cheddar macaroni and cheese.

The Trader Joe's version of the creamy comfort dish has ingredients that match Annie's almost exactly. If the ingredient similarities are not evidence enough, a packaging mistake in 2026 sealed the deal. Several customers posted photos online after allegedly opening their Trader Joe's Organic Shells and White Cheddar macaroni and cheese, only to find Annie's branded white cheddar powdered cheese packets inside. Whoops. That all but confirms it for sure.

Trader Joe's customers have expressed a lot of thoughts online about the store's meat and poultry selection. Some prefer it over what they find elsewhere, while others suggest it is expensive and subpar. But, like the other private label products at Trader Joe's, it may be the same meat and poultry you've bought elsewhere under a different name.

Customers who believed the fan favorite Trader Joe's Sweet Apple Chicken Sausage was a convincing dupe for Al Fresco's version were vindicated in 2015 when a recall of Kayem chicken sausages affected both brands. At the time, both Trader Joe's Sweet Apple Chicken Sausage and Al Fresco Apple Maple Chicken Breakfast Sausage were recalled due to the possibility of contamination with small pieces of plastic.

Whether Kayem still supplies the sausages is unclear, though the Trader Joe's website suggests the sausages are unchanged since they were introduced in 2004. The October 2026 recall of over 1.5 million pounds of ready-to-eat Kayem products due to improper storage temperature does not include any Trader Joe's branded products as of this writing.

Falling in love with a seasonal tea at Trader Joe's, only to have it discontinued is a terrible feeling. Many customers have found what they believe is a workaround. Several social media threads suggest Celestial Seasonings produces Trader Joe's tea, and that you can often order even the seasonal varieties year-round.

One of the most convincing arguments is a Reddit thread that focuses on Trader Joe's Candy Cane green tea. Not only are the ingredients identical to Celestial Seasonings Candy Cane Lane green tea, the boxes bear a striking resemblance with green clad polar bears on the front and the same box shape and design. Customers also suggest that Trader Joe's discontinued Red Refresh herbal tea is almost identical to Red Zinger by Celestial Seasonings in taste, description, and packaging.

One commenter alleges that they personally saw Trader Joe's mango tea boxes when they went on the Celestial Seasonings factory tour and recounts being told by the tour guide that Celestial Seasonings makes other teas for the retailer. What we know for sure is that Celestial Seasonings publicly partnered with Trader Joe's for two exclusive tea blends in 2013 (Harvest Blend and Chai). While the company's website previously noted this as a milestone event on its history page (via Internet Archive), the information has since been removed.

Comparing Trader Joe's thin and crunchy pretzel slims with Snack Factory's original pretzel crisps, there are certainly some compelling similarities among the ingredients. Trader Joe's pretzel slims contain unbleached enriched flour, inverted sugar syrup, salt, malted barley, sodium bicarbonate (baking soda), and sodium hydroxide. Snack Factory's pretzel crisps contain enriched flour, cane sugar, salt, tapioca malt syrup, canola oil, and [baking] soda. The two varieties also share a 1-ounce serving size with matching calorie content. Thankfully, Snack Factory's dark chocolate variety is easier to find than Trader Joe's.

There's nothing like a bowl of warm soup in the fall and winter months, and few soups are as resoundingly praised as Trader Joe's organic tomato and roasted red pepper soup. Customers rave about eating the soup with grilled cheese sandwiches, macaroni and cheese balls, or even with a bit of rice mixed in to bulk it up as a standalone meal. If that has you craving a bowl for yourself but your Trader Joe's doesn't have any in stock, just pick up a carton of Pacific Food's roasted red pepper and tomato soup. A 2017 recall due to under-processing revealed they are both made by Pacific.

Although other varieties of Trader Joe's soups have not been recalled, and we therefore do not have a confirmation as to their manufacturer, the same style box that is used for the organic tomato and roasted red pepper soup (and Pacific soups) is also used for the store's organic chicken and vegetable broths, including regular and low sodium.

For folks with peanut allergies, Trader Joe's Dark Chocolate Almond Butter Cups can be a great alternative to the more common peanut butter cups. Unfortunately, a 2021 recall revealed that some of the almond butter cups might have inadvertently contained peanut protein. While the package label indicated traces of peanuts were possible, allergic reactions prompted the recall anyway. The recall also revealed the candy was produced by Bazzini.

Even if you don't know the name, you likely know the products. Bazzini started out in 1886, making it the oldest nut and confection company in the United States, and also the brand of peanuts sold at Yankee Stadium. Its chocolate confections are sold under the name Barton's and include not only dark chocolate almond butter cups, but also milk chocolate peanut butter cups and dark chocolate peanut butter cups. Both peanut butter cup varieties are also available at Trader Joe's and may also be produced by Bazzini.

Trader Joe's selection of snack foods is arguably only matched by its selection of frozen foods and meals, especially when it comes to international cuisine. It might not be too surprising to learn that the manufacturer behind at least some of these international frozen foods is Ajinomoto Foods, which purports to be the brand leader in the sector.

While we can't definitively say all the different products Ajinomoto provides to Trader Joe's, a large recall in early 2026 included Trader Joe's chicken fried rice. The recall was initially issued due to the possibility of glass fragments in several products across many different labels. Trader Joe's expanded on Ajinomoto's initial recall and included its vegetable fried rice, Japanese fried rice, and chicken Shu Mai to be on the safe side, confirming that all are Ajinomoto products. All of those are pretty popular TJ's products, too.

For those of us who love yogurt, Trader Joe's has plenty to choose from, and it's one of the few products whose origin is somewhat easy to pinpoint, even without a specific recall. In 2017, a writer for Fortune revealed that Stonyfield supplies Trader Joe's with a good deal of its yogurt, especially on the East Coast. Around the same time, a Trader Joe's employee confirmed Stonyfield was one of the store's partners during a Reddit Ask Me Anything session.

Even though Stonyfield had one of the worst yogurt recalls in history, that was also all the way back in 2017 and applied only to plant-based yogurt, none of which was recalled from Trader Joe's. But tracking the manufacturer of Trader Joe's yogurt is a lot easier than some other products due to the ease with which consumers can track dairy manufacturing in the United States using the website Where Is My Milk From.

Dairy plant codes used by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) are stamped on all containers and can be traced to specific manufacturers. For example, Trader Joe's yogurt with dairy codes that begin with 33-14 originate at the Stonyfield plant in Londonderry, New Hampshire.

The holiday season is one of the best times of the year for foodies because all sorts of seasonal gourmet condiments and snacks start to hit the shelves at Trader Joe's. Among these are jams, jellies, spreads, and bar mixes, all of which can be perfect additions to holiday celebrations.

The problem is that once they're gone, they're gone. That is, unless you are a discerning customer who is able to figure out that Trader Joe's Step Up to the Snack Bar mix, discontinued garlic and onion jam, and pepper jelly are all dead ringers for the same products at Stonewall Kitchen. In particular, Trader Joe's and Stonewall Kitchen's bar mixes both contain honey roasted peanuts, honey mustard pretzels, cheddar crackers, sesame sticks, and chili lemon sticks.

Unfortunately, neither the garlic and onion jam nor the pepper jelly are currently available at Trader Joe's, but they've been known to make a comeback seasonally. If you simply can't wait, Stonewall Kitchen sells them year-round.

A living trust is a legal arrangement where you (the grantor) transfer ownership of your assets to a trust entity that you also control (as trustee). It sounds circular, and in practice, during your lifetime, nothing changes about how you use your money and property. The magic happens when you die or become incapacitated.

During your lifetime: You are both the grantor and the trustee. You control everything. You can add or remove assets, change beneficiaries, modify terms, or dissolve the trust entirely. Your Social Security number is the trust's tax ID — there is no separate tax return. For practical purposes, nothing changes about your daily financial life.

If you become incapacitated: Your successor trustee immediately takes over management of trust assets. No court petition needed. No guardianship proceeding. No delay. This is a major advantage over a will, which provides zero protection during incapacity.

When you die: Your successor trustee distributes assets according to your trust document. No probate court. No public record. No waiting 6-18 months. Beneficiaries can typically receive assets within days or weeks.

A living trust essentially creates a private, self-executing transfer system that operates outside the court system entirely. For FI families who have spent years building wealth, this means your heirs receive the full value of your estate without probate eating into it.

The terms "revocable" and "irrevocable" describe whether you can change or dissolve the trust after creating it. This distinction has major implications for control, taxes, and asset protection.

Revocable living trust — the standard choice for most families:

You retain full control. You can amend the trust, add or remove assets, change beneficiaries, or dissolve it completely at any time. Because you maintain control, the IRS treats trust assets as yours — they are included in your taxable estate, and creditors can reach them. The primary benefit is probate avoidance and incapacity protection, not asset protection or tax reduction.

Irrevocable trust — the advanced tool for specific situations:

Once created, you generally cannot change or revoke it. You give up control of the assets placed inside. In exchange, you get benefits that a revocable trust cannot provide.

For most FI families: A revocable living trust is the right starting point. It provides the two biggest benefits — probate avoidance and incapacity protection — while letting you maintain complete control.

Creating a trust document is only half the job. A trust only controls assets that are titled in its name. An unfunded trust is a worthless piece of paper.

Assets you should transfer into your trust:

The re-titling process for real estate: This is the most critical step and requires recording a new deed. You transfer ownership from "John Smith" to "John Smith, Trustee of the John Smith Revocable Living Trust dated January 15, 2024." Contact your county recorder's office or have your attorney prepare the deed. Most counties charge $15-$75 for recording. Notify your mortgage company (they cannot call the loan due under the Garn-St. Germain Act for transfers to a revocable trust) and your homeowners insurance carrier.

Ongoing funding discipline: Every time you open a new bank account, buy property, or acquire significant assets, ask: "Should this be titled in my trust?" Create a simple checklist and review it annually. The most common estate planning failure is a perfectly drafted trust with assets still titled in the grantor's personal name.

A common concern is whether transferring your home into a trust triggers a due-on-sale clause in your mortgage. Under the federal Garn-St. Germain Depository Institutions Act of 1982, lenders cannot accelerate a mortgage when property is transferred to a revocable trust where the borrower remains a beneficiary and occupant. This protection applies to residential properties with fewer than five units. Your lender may ask for a copy of the trust document, but they cannot call the loan. Always notify your homeowners insurance company of the title change to ensure coverage remains valid.

A living trust is most valuable if your net worth exceeds $500K, you own property in multiple states, you want to avoid probate, or you want incapacity protection. If your estate is simple and under $500K, a will may be sufficient.

Online services (Trust & Will $399-$599, LegalZoom $399-$599) work for simple trusts. For complex situations or estates over $1M, an estate planning attorney ($1,500-$5,000) ensures proper drafting and funding.

Your trust document should name your trustee (you), successor trustee, beneficiaries, and detailed distribution instructions. Include provisions for incapacity and specific instructions for each major asset category.

Transfer real estate by recording new deeds. Retitle bank and brokerage accounts into the trust name. Complete the assignment of personal property document. This is the most critical step — an unfunded trust is useless.

Draft a pour-over will that directs any assets not in the trust to pour into it upon your death. This will also names guardians for minor children. Review and update both documents every 3-5 years.

A living trust is a legal entity you create during your lifetime that holds your assets. You serve as trustee and maintain full control. When you die or become incapacitated, a successor trustee you named manages and distributes assets to your beneficiaries — without probate or court involvement.

A revocable living trust costs $1,500-$3,000 through an estate planning attorney, or $399-$599 through online services like Trust & Will or LegalZoom. Irrevocable trusts cost $3,000-$10,000+ due to their complexity. Additional costs include deed preparation ($200-$500) for transferring real estate.

A revocable living trust does NOT reduce estate taxes — assets are still part of your taxable estate because you maintain control. Only irrevocable trusts remove assets from your taxable estate. However, with the federal estate tax exemption at $13.61 million per individual (2024), estate taxes only affect very large estates.

Yes, and you should be. With a revocable living trust, you serve as your own trustee during your lifetime. You maintain complete control over all trust assets — buying, selling, spending, and investing exactly as you did before. Your successor trustee only takes over upon your death or incapacity.

A will goes through probate court (public, 6-18 months, costs 3-7% of estate). A living trust avoids probate entirely (private, days to weeks, minimal cost). A trust also provides incapacity protection, which a will does not. However, a will can name guardians for minor children, which a trust cannot.

Yes. You need a pour-over will to catch any assets not titled in the trust and to name guardians for minor children. The trust handles your major assets and avoids probate. The will serves as a safety net for everything else.

#9675. Not Milk: Burgers Are 10x Juicier When You Add This Ingredient

Chefs employ many strategies to moisten burger patties. Some add a dash of mayo for extra fat and flavor, while others swear by heavy cream for juicy patties. Still, there are always more mouth-watering options to explore — like buttermilk, for example. The tangy fermented dairy is often designated for giving pancakes some fluff, but lends advantages when worked into minced meat, too.

The lactic acid in buttermilk functions as an effective meat tenderizer, making a burger that's a touch juicier. The dairy's tartness is perceptible in the taste without overwhelming the palate. You don't need much to revamp a burger recipe; half a cup per a pound of beef is enough to translate buttermilk's unique effects. Simply mix and form the patties like during a traditional burger recipe, folding in supplementary ingredients like onions and breadcrumbs if desired.

Similar results in texture and flavor are also possible with buttermilk powder. The dehydrated version of the dairy is easier to work with, and still contains the signature fat and tanginess, just without the extra water. It effectively creates a crust around meats, making it widely used in Southern dry rubs. Dust a third of a cup onto a pound of meat, and you'll get a juicy burger, while helping seasonings stick. Who knew buttermilk could prove so valuable on burger night?

While the effects are primarily textural, buttermilk impacts the burger's flavor, too. The inclusion adds a lightly acidic and milky taste, setting up for complementary ingredients. You can further lean into the patty's tender flavor by adding breadcrumbs, which yield an extra-tender, meatball-like dish. Consider using a flavored crumb — say Italian-herb — and work onions and pickles into the patty, too. Topped with ingredients like fresh basil and sliced tomatoes, you'll get an extra-juicy burger that's enjoyable even when well-done.

Alternatively, you can steer the tanginess into a more spiced direction. Buttermilk is widely used in Indian cooking to absorb aromatics and the same kind of application works in a burger. Mix in store-bought curry powder or make your own blend using aromatics like cumin, coriander, and ginger. To round out the dish, top with mango chutney or a fragrant chile paste.

Finally, if you'd like to keep your burger rendition on the classic side, consider garnishing with a homemade ranch. The iconic sauce employs buttermilk, too, making a burger rendition flavored with the dairy both inside and out. Optionally paired with a couple of bacon strips, it's a flavorful riff on the dish that's bound to stay moist.

#9673. One Can Of Sweetened Condensed Milk Is The Start To This Easy Brazilian Dessert

Many desserts can be intimidatingly complex, requiring both difficult technique and extensive ingredients. That need not always be the case, though. For a delicious batch of brigadeiros – an iconic Brazilian dessert – preparation starts with a simple can of sweetened condensed milk. The sweet is essentially like a chewy chocolate truffle, constructed using a trio of cocoa powder, butter, and the cornerstone condensed milk. The assembly is as straightforward as the ingredients. All components are simmered together over low heat for around twenty minutes to thicken, then cooled and formed into bite-sized balls.

Although easy to make, the dessert is delicious and playful. The condensed milk lends each bite a signature caramel-like sweetness, balanced out by the cocoa bitterness. The dessert is made to a soft consistency, but often coated with fun garnishes like chocolate sprinkles, nuts, or coconut flakes, yielding an intriguing textural contrast. Arranged on a plate, it's a surprising way to use condensed milk with an impressive result.

With Brigidiaro's three-ingredient composition, every element plays a role in the final flavor. Not all cans of sweetened condensed milk are alike. Some taste sweeter, others more caramel-forward, all while varying in texture, too. As the sole source of sugar in the dessert, the type you choose defines its sweetness. For example, regular granulated sugar is a blank canvas, ready to take on the cocoa flavor while brown sugars have a little note of molasses. Want to fine-tune the brigidiaro even further? Consider making your own sweetened condensed milk at home using solely milk and sugar.

In parallel, the employed cocoa powder also makes a noticeable difference. The foodstuff's treatment influences the taste –  a Dutch process will feature less acidity, for example. And for even more control over the Brigidairo's chocolate taste, consider shaving a chocolate bar, one of the easiest substitutes for cocoa powder. With such an inclusion, you can vary the cocoa composition. An 85% cocoa powder will lend the brigidairo more complex dark and earthy notes, while a milder 50% makes for an extra sweet and creamy experience.

Butter serves as a fat that brings the components together. Go for a classic unsalted stick; there's no need for an extra flavorful cultured butter or a higher-fat European-style. And once the fat has melted, you could optionally stir in flavorings like lemon juice and zest (use white chocolate or skip it altogether for this) or spices such as nutmeg and cinnamon to add subtle warmth throughout your dessert. All held together with a three-ingredient foundation, brigadeiros welcome a multitude of subtle twists.

#9671. Heavy cream vs. whipping cream: What's the difference?: Understanding the right cream for your baking.

If you’re baking a recipe that calls for heavy cream, or picking up a carton to turn into whipped cream to finish a dessert, you may be confused when you hit the dairy aisle. There’s “heavy cream” — but also “heavy whipping cream” or, in some cases, just “whipping cream.”

So when it comes to heavy cream versus whipping cream, is there truly a difference?

Aside from being delicious, there are very specific definitions and standards that must be met in order for something to be labeled as heavy cream. It is made by separating the fatty top layer from the base milk layer during processing. The FDA states that heavy cream is cream that contains no less than 36% milk fat.  Comparatively, milk has 0% to around 3% milk fat, as well as a higher water concentration. Because of its fat content, heavy cream retains a rich taste and, when whipped, it excels at creating stiff peaks that hold their shape for a long time.

Whipping cream — sometimes called “heavy whipping cream” — is made using a similar process as heavy cream and is also the milk fat removed before milk is homogenized. However, whipping cream can contain somewhere between 30% and 35% milk fat content, according to FDA regulations. Because of its slightly lower fat content, it whips into a softer, more billowy cream, and it will deflate more quickly than whipped cream made with heavy cream.

Luckily, the difference in taste and performance between the two types of cream are not very discernible. This means you can use them interchangeably in recipes — and it's okay if you accidentally buy the "wrong" one. Both can yield a delicious bowl of homemade whipped cream. (Can’t justify buying a whole carton of either one? We’ve got you covered with an easy homemade heavy cream substitute.)

A note on King Arthur recipes: The King Arthur Test Kitchen prefers heavy cream in most instances, particularly when making whipped cream, because of the higher fat content. That said, you can substitute heavy whipping cream 1:1 in any King Arthur recipe that calls specifically for heavy cream without any issue.

As a general rule of thumb, use heavy cream for making stable whipped cream for topping pies, layered desserts like tiramisu or banana pudding, and any sweet where the structural integrity hinges on the cream really holding its shape. Heavy cream can also be handy for making cream scones and drop biscuits, where the richness of the dairy can shine through. For more heavy cream baking inspiration, check out these 12 recipes that call on heavy cream.

#9669. For Heartier Scrambled Eggs, Make Them Rolex-Style

Scrambled eggs make for a reliable breakfast option, but turning them into a hearty meal can be tricky. Sure, there's always the tried-and-true eggs on toast à la tartine, or a classic side of hash browns. However, to really shake up your breakfast routine, look toward the Ugandan rolex. This popular street food rolls up eggs into chapati (an unleavened flatbread), supplemented with flavorful vegetable additions. Wrapped up into a swirled shape, it's a dish reminiscent of a breakfast taco, only with an East African appeal all of its own.

Assembly starts like many an egg dish: The cornerstone ingredient is whisked in a bowl (although it can also be stirred in a pan for a change of texture). All the while, a variable vegetable medley consisting of ingredients like onion, tomatoes, spicy chiles, cabbage, and occasionally garlic softens in a pan. The eggs go into the veggie mix, are allowed to set, and are then rolled into already warmed flatbread.

Some construct the dish right in the pan; others on a separate plate. Either way, it's crucial to give the flatbread a tight roll — more than with a breakfast taco — creasing the dish over two to three times. Flavorful, handheld, and open to many modifications, a rolex (a play on the band of the watch and "rolled eggs") makes for a great addition to the morning rotation.

In Uganda — especially the capital, Kampala — rolex rolls are made by a multitude of vendors, each adding a unique spin. As a result, feel free to work in your own customizations, whether into the vegetable mix or as a condiment topping on top. Tomatoes, pepper, cabbage, and onion form the most frequent foundation, but you can also add carrots for textural enhancement. You can also enhance the flavor using aromatics like garlic, ginger, scallions, as well as fresh herbs like cilantro or parsley. You could even have an Asian-inspired riff and throw in some nori, chilli crunch, and mirin.

In addition to the vegetable filling, spiff out your rolex right before rolling. Opt for one of the cheeses that's a perfect addition to scrambled eggs for an ooey-gooey bite; Swiss or feta is a reliable choice. And to give the dish a more American flair, strips of bacon add to the heartiness. There's no such thing as too many components, so long as the roll stays intact. Traditionally, the dish is eaten handheld, wrapped in plastic on-the-go, so just make sure any additional ingredients sit securely in the eggs and flatbread.
